politics.text: Three hundred Spartans and their Greek allies hold the pass at Thermopylae against the huge Persian army of King Xerxes.
politics.context: The stand lasted three days in late summer. King Leonidas died with his men, after most of the allies had been sent away.

society.text: The Athenians abandon their city and flee to the island of Salamis, and the Persians burn the Acropolis.
society.context: It happened in the late summer, shortly before the Greek naval victory at Salamis.

technology.text: Persian engineers lash hundreds of ships together to bridge the Hellespont, so that Xerxes' huge army can cross from Asia into Europe.
technology.context: Herodotus describes the bridges, and says that an earlier pair was destroyed by a storm.

arts_culture.text: The playwright Aeschylus fights in the Greek fleet at the Battle of Salamis, an experience he later turns into his play The Persians.
arts_culture.context: The Persians was staged in 472 BCE and is the oldest Greek tragedy that survives.

politics.text: Cincinnatus, called from his farm to be dictator of Rome, beats the Aequi at Mount Algidus and then resigns his office.
politics.context: Livy says he gave up power sixteen days after the battle and went back to his plough. The story is partly legend, and he became a Roman model of civic duty.

society.text: Athens opens its top office, the archonship, to poorer citizens, extending the democratic reforms of Ephialtes.
society.context: The archonship had been limited to the wealthy. The year page credits Pericles, but the reform is often dated a year later.

technology.text: Athenians begin building the Long Walls, which link their city to its port of Piraeus to protect its food supply.
technology.context: The walls let Athens hold out against a siege as long as its navy kept the sea route open. Construction took several years.

arts_culture.text: Aeschylus presents the Oresteia, the only complete Greek tragic trilogy to survive, at the Athenian festival of Dionysus.
arts_culture.context: The three plays are Agamemnon, The Libation Bearers and The Eumenides, which end with the founding of a court in Athens. Aeschylus died a few years later in Sicily.

politics.text: The Qin general Sima Cuo marches through Bashu and conquers part of the state of Chu in western Qianzhong.
politics.context: Qin kept gaining ground on its rivals and went on to unify China within two generations.

society.text: The Roman envoy Fabricius refuses a bribe from Pyrrhus, and Pyrrhus frees Roman prisoners without ransom.
society.context: Later writers made Fabricius a model of Roman honesty. The exchange followed the battle of Heraclea.

technology.text: At Heraclea, Pyrrhus's war elephants terrify the Roman horses and help him win, the first time Romans faced them.
technology.context: Pyrrhus won but lost many men. The Romans later learned to defeat elephants with fire and javelins.

arts_culture.text: The Colossus of Rhodes, a bronze statue of the sun god Helios over thirty metres tall, is finished after about twelve years.
arts_culture.context: The sculptor was Chares of Lindos. The statue stood for only about half a century before an earthquake brought it down.

politics.text: Conspirators in the southern Italian city of Tarentum let Hannibal's army in, and the Carthaginian general takes the city.
politics.context: Tarentum had been a Roman ally. Rome kept hold of the citadel and won the city back a few years later.

society.text: Rome elects Publius Licinius Crassus as its chief priest, the pontifex maximus, an office he will hold for nearly thirty years.
society.context: The pontifex maximus led Rome's state religion and kept its calendar. Crassus was a rich noble and held the post until his death.

technology.text: The Romans under Marcellus take Syracuse, which had held them off with Archimedes' catapults, cranes and ship-lifting claws.
technology.context: The claw was a crane-like arm that lifted ships and dropped them. The siege began the year before. Archimedes was killed in the sack, on a date that is uncertain.

arts_culture.text: Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China, begins work on the vast Epang Palace near his capital.
arts_culture.context: The palace was never finished. A later tradition says the rebel Xiang Yu burned it down, but historians doubt the story.

politics.text: Julius Caesar storms the Gallic town of Avaricum after a hard siege, and his legionaries slaughter its people.
politics.context: Avaricum is now Bourges in France. It fell in March, during the Gallic revolt led by Vercingetorix. Caesar's own account says almost no one inside escaped.

society.text: Publius Clodius Pulcher, a popular Roman politician, is murdered on the Appian Way by the followers of his rival Milo.
society.context: It happened in January. His death set off riots in Rome, and Milo was later put on trial for it.

technology.text: Caesar's army digs two huge rings of siege works around Alesia, trapping Vercingetorix inside and holding off a Gallic relief army.
technology.context: One ring faced the town and the other faced outwards, with trenches, towers and forts. It was fought in the autumn. Archaeologists doubt the lines were unbroken.

arts_culture.text: The Roman orator Cicero rises to defend Milo on a murder charge, but the crowd and soldiers rattle him and the defence fails.
arts_culture.context: Cicero later wrote out the speech he wished he had given. It became a model of Latin oratory. Milo went into exile.

politics.text: Octavian ferries his legions across the sea to Greece to fight Mark Antony, while his friend Agrippa takes command of the fleet.
politics.context: It opened the last war of the Roman civil wars. Antony had Cleopatra of Egypt as his ally.

society.text: A violent earthquake strikes Judea, killing many people and wrecking buildings in the lands ruled by King Herod.
society.context: The Jewish historian Josephus describes it, and geologists have found traces of it around the Dead Sea.

technology.text: In a great sea battle off Greece, Octavian's admiral Agrippa uses a catapult-fired grapnel, the harpax, to snare and board Antony's ships.
technology.context: The battle was Actium, fought in September. Antony's ships were bigger, but Octavian's smaller ships were quicker. Antony and Cleopatra fled.

arts_culture.text: In southern India, the poet Tiruvalluvar is born, by Tamil tradition. He will write the Tirukkural, a famous book of couplets on ethics.
arts_culture.context: This date is traditional, and historians place him much later. The Tamil Thiruvalluvar calendar still counts its years from it.

politics.text: The Roman general Marcus Agrippa crushes the last resistance in northern Spain, completing Rome's conquest of the Iberian peninsula.
politics.context: The Cantabrian Wars had lasted about ten years. Rome now ruled all of Iberia.

society.text: King Herod the Great begins rebuilding the Temple in Jerusalem on a grand scale.
society.context: The work began around this time and went on for decades. The Romans destroyed the finished Temple in the year 70 CE.

technology.text: The Romans complete the Aqua Virgo, an aqueduct that carries clear spring water to the baths and fountains of Rome.
technology.context: Agrippa built it. Parts of it still supply the Trevi Fountain today.

arts_culture.text: The Roman poet Virgil dies, leaving his epic poem the Aeneid unfinished.
arts_culture.context: He asked for it to be burned, but Emperor Augustus ordered it published. It became Rome's national epic.

politics.text: Titus becomes Roman emperor on the death of his father, Vespasian.
politics.context: Vespasian died in June. Titus reigned for only two years.

society.text: Mount Vesuvius erupts and buries the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and mud.
society.context: The traditional date is in August, though some evidence points to the autumn. Thousands died, and the towns lay buried for about sixteen centuries.

technology.text: The Roman writer and naturalist Pliny the Elder dies while sailing across the bay to rescue people and study the eruption of Vesuvius.
technology.context: His nephew, Pliny the Younger, described the eruption in two famous letters.

arts_culture.text: Han scholars gather at the White Tiger Hall, in Luoyang, to debate the Confucian classics, and the record becomes a famous book.
arts_culture.context: Emperor Zhang called the conference to settle disputes over how to read the classics. The book is called the Baihu Tong.

politics.text: Simon bar Kokhba leads a Jewish revolt against Emperor Hadrian and Roman rule in Judea, and briefly sets up an independent state.
politics.context: The revolt lasted about three years. Hadrian's legions crushed it, and Rome then renamed the province Syria Palaestina.

society.text: Merchants, innkeepers and craftsmen build villages outside the forts of Hadrian's Wall to serve the Roman soldiers.
society.context: Such civilian settlements, called vici, grew beside the forts. The source dates this only to the year, so check it.

technology.text: The Chinese court astronomer Zhang Heng builds a bronze seismoscope, decorated with dragons and toads, that senses distant earthquakes.
technology.context: A pendulum inside the vessel made a ball drop from a dragon's mouth into a toad's, which showed the direction of the quake. He served the Han court at Luoyang. The date is traditional.

arts_culture.text: The Temple of Olympian Zeus in Athens, begun more than six centuries earlier, is finished at last under the emperor Hadrian.
arts_culture.context: Work began under the Athenian tyrant Peisistratos and then stopped for centuries. Hadrian dedicated the finished temple. Some sources give the year before.

politics.text: Pope Agatho is the first pope to stop paying a tribute to the Byzantine emperor Constantine IV on being elected.
politics.context: Agatho succeeded Donus in the spring. The payment had long reflected the emperor's hold over Rome, so stopping it was a sign of the papacy's growing independence.

society.text: Emperor Tenmu's daughter Princess Tōchi, chosen as priestess to the gods, dies days before a planned sacrifice.
society.context: Tenmu had planned a national ritual to honour the gods of heaven and earth, and had to cancel the sacrifice. She was buried about a week later, possibly at Akō.

technology.text: Byzantine ships burn an Arab fleet off Sillyon with Greek fire, a flammable liquid sprayed at the enemy through tubes.
technology.context: The victory helped end the Arab siege of Constantinople. The recipe was a closely guarded state secret and is now lost. Its first use may fall a few years earlier.

arts_culture.text: The monk Uisang is traditionally said to found Beomeosa, a Buddhist temple, under King Munmu of the Korean kingdom of Silla.
arts_culture.context: The temple stands on Geumjeong mountain, in the modern city of Busan, and is still active. The founding date is traditional.

politics.text: Pepin the Short forces the last Merovingian king into a monastery and is crowned king of the Franks, with the pope's blessing.
politics.context: Pope Zachary had agreed that the man with the real power should be king. Pepin's son was Charlemagne.

politics.text: An Abbasid army beats a Tang Chinese army at the Battle of Talas in Central Asia, in a clash between two great empires.
politics.context: The Abbasids stopped China's spread to the west. A famous story says Chinese prisoners taught Muslims papermaking, but historians dispute it.

society.text: In Korea, the Silla minister Kim Daeseong orders the building of the Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto at Gyeongju.
society.context: Both are now UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Seokguram holds a famous stone Buddha. Kim died before they were finished.

technology.text: Paper is said to be made for the first time in the Islamic world, in Samarkand, after Chinese papermakers are captured at Talas.
technology.context: Samarkand became a famous centre of paper-making, and paper then spread west. Some historians doubt the story, and think paper reached Samarkand earlier.

arts_culture.text: The huge bronze Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji in Nara, Japan, is finished.
arts_culture.context: It was cast in sections. The ceremony to open the statue's eyes was held in 752. Its hall is one of the largest wooden buildings in the world.

politics.text: William Rufus crushes a revolt led by his uncle, Bishop Odo of Bayeux, after sieges at Pevensey and Rochester castles.
politics.context: Odo was the Conqueror's half-brother. Rufus took his lands and sent him into exile in Normandy. Nobles across England had joined the revolt.

society.text: The University of Bologna is founded, by later tradition, and goes on to be the oldest university still teaching today.
society.context: The date was fixed centuries afterwards, when scholars marked the university's anniversary. Bologna began as a centre for teaching law.

technology.text: In Kaifeng, Su Song builds a model of his water-driven astronomical clock tower, with an escapement and a chain drive.
technology.context: The chain drive is the oldest known way of transmitting power. The finished tower, built a few years later, turned an armillary sphere and had mechanical figures that showed the hours on plaques.

arts_culture.text: The Chinese scholar Shen Kuo writes the Dream Pool Essays, notes that record the magnetic compass and movable type.
arts_culture.context: The book also covers astronomy, geology and optics. The date of the finished text is approximate.

politics.text: Emperor Manuel Komnenos marries sixteen-year-old Maria of Antioch in the church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.
politics.context: Maria was a princess from the Crusader state of Antioch. Their son, Alexios the Second, became emperor as a boy and was murdered as a young teenager.

society.text: Edward the Confessor, who rebuilt Westminster Abbey, is declared a saint by Pope Alexander the Third.
society.context: The canonisation was in January, nearly a century after his death. His body was later moved to a new shrine in the abbey.

technology.text: At Caishi on the Yangtze, Song paddle-wheel warships and gunpowder bombs smash a larger Jin fleet.
technology.context: Chinese accounts say the bombs were thrown by trebuchets and burst with a loud noise and a cloud of lime. The defeat helped end the Jin emperor's invasion, and his own officers killed him weeks later.

arts_culture.text: The jeweller Lazar Bohsha makes a jewelled cross for Euphrosyne of Polotsk, later one of Belarus's great lost treasures.
arts_culture.context: The cross held relics and was kept for centuries. It disappeared during the Second World War and has never been found.

politics.text: Muhammad I is elected ruler of Arjona in Spain and founds the Nasrid dynasty, the last Muslim rulers of Iberia.
politics.context: He had rebelled against Ibn Hud. He later took Granada and began building the Alhambra. His dynasty lasted until the end of the fifteenth century.

society.text: Troyes issues the first recorded life annuities, a way for a town to raise money by borrowing from its citizens.
society.context: A buyer paid a lump sum and received payments for life. Reims had started the trend of public borrowing some years earlier.

technology.text: Defenders of Kaifeng hurl iron bombs packed with gunpowder, the thunder-crash bombs, at the besieging Mongols.
technology.context: The Jin History records blasts that killed attackers, and the defenders also used fire lances. The Mongols broke off the siege after several weeks but took the city the next year.

arts_culture.text: Mongol invaders burn the wooden printing blocks of the Tripitaka Koreana, Korea's first great set of Buddhist scriptures.
arts_culture.context: The blocks were kept at Buin Temple near Daegu. Korea carved a second set in the following decades. It survives at Haeinsa temple and is a World Heritage site.

politics.text: English barons, angry at the costly foreign schemes of King Henry III, force him to accept a council to share in ruling the kingdom.
politics.context: The reforms are known as the Provisions of Oxford. They were an early limit on royal power. The barons were led by nobles such as Simon de Montfort.

politics.text: Venetian and Genoese fleets fight a fierce sea battle off Acre in their long war over trade in the Crusader ports of the Holy Land.
politics.context: It is called the Battle of Acre. Venice won it, but the war between the two merchant cities went on for years.

society.text: The Republic of Genoa starts forcing its taxpayers to lend money to the state, through loans known as luoghi.
society.context: Forced loans like these were a common way for medieval cities to pay for their wars and public spending.

technology.text: Mongol siege engines under Hulagu Khan batter the walls of Baghdad until the capital of the Abbasid caliph surrenders.
technology.context: The engines breached the walls within a couple of days. The siege ran from late January to early February, and the Mongols entered the city days later.

arts_culture.text: Salisbury Cathedral, a graceful Gothic church in southern England, is consecrated.
arts_culture.context: It was built quickly and in one style. Its famous tall spire was added later. The consecration took place at the end of September.

arts_culture.text: Civil unrest in northern Italy gives rise to the Geisslerlieder, penitential songs sung by wandering bands of Flagellants.
arts_culture.context: Flagellants whipped themselves in public as penance. The name Geisslerlieder comes from the German word for flagellants.

politics.text: The Marinid sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub enters Ceuta peacefully, ending about four decades of local independence.
politics.context: Ceuta lies on the North African coast across the strait from Spain. The source gives no date within the year.

society.text: Edward I orders a great survey of land and landholders in England, later known as the Hundred Rolls.
society.context: Royal commissioners asked each hundred who held land and what rights the crown had lost. It is often compared with the Domesday survey.

technology.text: Mongol-led invaders land at Hakata Bay in Japan and hurl exploding bombs at the samurai before a storm wrecks their fleet.
technology.context: The fleet had first taken Tsushima and Iki. A later scroll painting shows samurai under the blasts. Sources say about thirteen thousand of thirty thousand men did not return.

arts_culture.text: In Florence, nine-year-old Dante Alighieri first sees Beatrice Portinari, who later guides him through Paradise.
arts_culture.context: Dante wrote that he saw her in the spring and loved her for life, though they hardly spoke. He made her his guide in the Divine Comedy.

politics.text: Trần Hưng Đạo's Vietnamese army sinks the Mongol-led fleet on the Bạch Đằng River, using iron-tipped stakes hidden in the riverbed.
politics.context: It was fought in April. The falling tide trapped the Yuan ships on the stakes. The defeat ended Kublai Khan's attempts to conquer Vietnam.

society.text: Bishop Petrus of Västerås buys an eighth of the Stora Kopparberg copper mine in Sweden, perhaps the oldest recorded company share.
society.context: The deal was made in June. The mine's owners later formed the company now called Stora Enso. Historians debate whether it was a true share.

technology.text: Yuan soldiers use a small bronze hand cannon, the oldest known, to put down the rebellion of the Mongol prince Nayan in Manchuria.
technology.context: The gun was found at Acheng, in Heilongjiang province. Its date comes from the fighting it is linked to, so it is approximate.

arts_culture.text: Work begins on Mob Quad at Merton College, Oxford, which becomes the oldest quadrangle in the university.
arts_culture.context: Work went on for decades, and the quadrangle is still part of the college today.

politics.text: A plot by Emperor Go-Daigo's supporters to overthrow the Kamakura shogunate is uncovered in Kyoto, in the Shōchū Incident.
politics.context: Go-Daigo wanted to restore direct imperial rule. He escaped punishment this time, but his next attempt led to his exile and, in the end, to the fall of the shogunate.

society.text: Mansa Musa, emperor of Mali, reaches Cairo on his pilgrimage to Mecca, bringing so much gold that its value drops for years.
society.context: He arrived in July. Writers in Cairo said he gave away so much gold that its price stayed low for over a decade. Accounts of the amounts vary.

technology.text: During the siege of Metz, in Lorraine, the attackers fire cannon at the city walls, a weapon described at the time as new.
technology.context: The siege began in September and the attackers withdrew by the end of the month. Whether this was really the first use of cannon in Europe is debated.

arts_culture.text: The Consistori del Gay Saber, a society of troubadour poets in Toulouse, holds its first poetry contest and awards a golden violet.
arts_culture.context: The first prize went to the poet Arnaut Vidal. The contest became the Jeux floraux, which is still held today.

politics.text: Qazaghan, a Turkic amir, kills Kazan Khan, and the Chagatai Khanate stops being a single state in Central Asia.
politics.context: Afterwards amirs ruled the lands and khans were puppets. The source gives no date within the year.

society.text: Ibn Battuta, a traveller from Morocco, reaches the Mongol-ruled Chinese capital in the middle of a civil war and riots.
society.context: He had left home on a pilgrimage to Mecca about two decades earlier and kept travelling. His dictated book describes the Yuan court. The date of his arrival varies between sources.

technology.text: At Crécy the English reportedly fire cannon at the French, said to be Europe's first gunpowder battle, but longbows win it.
technology.context: Historians dispute how many guns were used and whether they mattered. The French lost many nobles, including the blind King John of Bohemia, who fought as their ally.

arts_culture.text: Part of the great dome of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople collapses, and the Byzantines begin a long repair.
arts_culture.context: Earthquakes had weakened the structure. The repair took years, and the church had already stood for over seven centuries.

politics.text: The Central Asian conqueror Timur, known in the West as Tamerlane, dies at Otrar while leading his army to invade Ming China.
politics.context: He died in February, and sources differ on the exact day. His empire soon split between his son Shah Rukh and his grandson Khalil Sultan.

society.text: The Annals of Clonmacnoise record a chieftain dying from too much aqua vitae, the earliest known written mention of whiskey.
society.context: The chieftain was Richard Magranell. Aqua vitae means "water of life", and monks are thought to have distilled it in Ireland at that time. The record survives in a later translation.

technology.text: Admiral Zheng He sets sail from Suzhou with more than three hundred ships, the first Ming treasure fleet to cross the Indian Ocean.
technology.context: The fleet left in July with about twenty-seven thousand men. It went as far as India, and later voyages reached East Africa. The size of the ships is debated.

arts_culture.text: Christine de Pizan, an Italian-born writer at the French court, finishes The Book of the City of Ladies, defending women against insults.
arts_culture.context: She was one of the first women in Europe to earn her living as a writer. She imagined an allegorical city built and ruled by famous women.

politics.text: King Henry V of England and King Charles VI of France sign the Treaty of Troyes, making Henry heir to the French throne.
politics.context: It was signed in May. It disinherited Charles's own son, the future Charles VII, and was later overturned.

society.text: Hussite forces defeat a crusading army led by Emperor Sigismund at Vítkov Hill, outside Prague.
society.context: It was fought in July. The Hussites, led by Jan Žižka, followed the teachings of the reformer Jan Hus, who had been burned at the stake.

technology.text: Filippo Brunelleschi begins building the huge dome of Florence Cathedral, without the usual wooden frame to support it.
technology.context: The dome took sixteen years and about four million bricks. It is still the largest brick dome in the world.

arts_culture.text: China's Yongle Emperor completes the Forbidden City, in Beijing, a palace of nearly a thousand buildings.
arts_culture.context: The capital moved from Nanjing the next year. Emperors lived in the palace for almost five centuries.

politics.text: Ashikaga Yoshimochi, the fourth shogun of Japan, steps down in favour of his son Yoshikazu.
politics.context: Yoshikazu was still a teenager. He died within two years, and Yoshimochi took control again.

society.text: Admiral Hong Bao, a deputy of Zheng He, returns to China after a voyage to the waters of Indonesia and the Philippines.
society.context: Hong Bao was one of the eunuch admirals of the Ming treasure fleets. He returned in the autumn. Accounts of his route are debated.

technology.text: Venice sets up the first permanent plague hospital on an island in its lagoon, to keep the sick apart from the city.
technology.context: It stood on the island of Santa Maria di Nazareth, which gave the word lazaretto its name. Other cities copied the idea of isolating the sick and quarantining ships.

arts_culture.text: Giovanni Aurispa arrives in Venice from Byzantium with over two hundred Greek manuscripts, the largest collection yet.
arts_culture.context: He had spent about two years collecting them. Scholars in Italy were eager for ancient Greek texts.

politics.text: Cosimo de' Medici returns to Florence after a year in exile and begins his family's long rule of the city.
politics.context: He returned in October, welcomed by a new government. He never held an official title, but ruled through his friends and banking wealth.

society.text: Moderate Hussites defeat the radical Taborites at the Battle of Lipany, ending the bloodiest phase of the Hussite Wars.
society.context: It was fought in May. Both sides were Bohemian reformers, and the defeat ended the radicals' power.

technology.text: The Portuguese navigator Gil Eanes sails past Cape Bojador, off West Africa, which sailors had long feared to pass.
technology.context: He made the voyage for Prince Henry the Navigator. It opened the way for the long Portuguese voyages down the African coast.

arts_culture.text: The Flemish painter Jan van Eyck paints the Arnolfini Portrait, a couple in a richly detailed room, with a mirror at the back.
arts_culture.context: The mirror reflects two more figures and the painter himself. The picture is now in the National Gallery in London.

politics.text: Plague kills Imam al-Mansur Ali, ruler of the Zaidi state in Yemen, and his son and successor dies four weeks later.
politics.context: He died in February. The source gives plague as the cause.

society.text: Under the child Zhengtong Emperor, Ming China lets farmers in the south pay much of their grain tax in silver instead of grain.
society.context: The change is known as Gold Floral Silver. It helped make silver the main money of Ming China. The source dates it only to the year.

technology.text: Johannes Gutenberg, working in Strasbourg, begins the experiments with metal type that lead to the printing press.
technology.context: The date is approximate. Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz printed his famous Bible about twenty years later.

arts_culture.text: Pope Eugene IV consecrates Florence Cathedral, topped by Brunelleschi's finished dome, the largest brick dome ever built.
arts_culture.context: It happened on the twenty-fifth of March. The dome was built without wooden supports, and the lantern on top came later. Guillaume Dufay's motet for the occasion was sung at the ceremony.

politics.text: The French army defeats the English at the Battle of Castillon, ending the Hundred Years' War.
politics.context: It was fought in July. The English commander, John Talbot, was killed, and France kept every English possession except Calais.

politics.text: The Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captures Constantinople after a siege of about seven weeks, ending the Byzantine Empire.
politics.context: The city fell on the twenty-ninth of May. It became the Ottoman capital, later called Istanbul.

society.text: The Ottoman sultan converts Hagia Sophia, the great church of Constantinople, into a mosque.
society.context: This happened soon after the city's fall in the spring. It served as a mosque until it became a museum in the 1930s.

technology.text: Giant Ottoman cannon, cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban, batter the great walls of Constantinople.
technology.context: The biggest gun fired heavy stone balls and was slow to reload, but the walls had never faced anything like it.

arts_culture.text: The Florentine sculptor Donatello completes the bronze statue of the mercenary general Gattamelata, in Padua.
arts_culture.context: It was the first large bronze statue of a horseman since ancient Rome, and it became a model for later monuments.

politics.text: Richard, Duke of York, defeats the royal army at the First Battle of St Albans, the opening fight of the Wars of the Roses.
politics.context: It was fought in May. The battle was short, and King Henry VI was wounded and captured.

society.text: The Church opens a new inquiry to clear the name of Joan of Arc, more than twenty years after she was burned at the stake.
society.context: The new inquiry began in the autumn. It declared her trial unfair, and she was made a saint in 1920.

technology.text: Johannes Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz produces the first Bible printed with movable metal type.
technology.context: The Gutenberg Bible was ready around this year. It helped start the printing revolution in Europe.

arts_culture.text: The Italian painter and friar Fra Angelico dies in Rome.
arts_culture.context: He painted glowing frescoes in the San Marco convent in Florence. The Church declared him blessed in 1982.

politics.text: Sultan Husayn Bayqara captures Herat, and under his rule the city becomes a centre of Persian painting and poetry.
politics.context: He took the city in March and ruled for nearly four decades. The painter Bihzad and the poet Jami worked at his court.

society.text: Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, is born in the village of Talwandi, in the Punjab.
society.context: Talwandi is now Nankana Sahib, in Pakistan. Most Sikhs celebrate his birthday in November, but some old accounts give a spring date, so the day is traditional.

technology.text: The German printer Johann of Speyer sets up the first printing press in Venice, and is granted a five-year monopoly on printing there.
technology.context: He printed Cicero's letters and Pliny's Natural History. He died the next year, and the monopoly ended.

arts_culture.text: The Florentine scholar Marsilio Ficino finishes translating the complete works of Plato from Greek into Latin for the Medici.
arts_culture.context: Cosimo de' Medici had commissioned the work, and the family gave Ficino a villa to do it in. Sources put the finish at about this year.

politics.text: The Spanish monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella capture Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain.
politics.context: Granada fell on the second of January. It ended about seven centuries of Muslim rule in much of Spain.

politics.text: The Genoese navigator Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, makes landfall in the Caribbean, in what he believes is Asia.
politics.context: He landed in October, in the Bahamas, and went on to reach Cuba and Hispaniola. Four voyages followed.

society.text: Spain's monarchs order every Jew who will not convert to Christianity to leave the country, in the Alhambra Decree.
society.context: It was issued in March. Tens of thousands left, many for Portugal and the Ottoman Empire.

technology.text: The German navigator Martin Behaim finishes the Erdapfel, the oldest surviving terrestrial globe, in Nuremberg.
technology.context: It shows no Americas, because it was made before news of Columbus's voyage arrived.

arts_culture.text: The Italian painter Piero della Francesca, a master of perspective and geometry, dies in Borgo San Sepolcro.
arts_culture.context: He died on the twelfth of October, the same day that Columbus first sighted land.

arts_culture.text: The Spanish scholar Antonio de Nebrija publishes the first grammar of the Spanish language.
arts_culture.context: It was presented to Queen Isabella. Nebrija is said to have told her that language is the companion of empire.

politics.text: Spain and Portugal sign the Treaty of Tordesillas, dividing the lands outside Europe between them.
politics.context: It was agreed in June. A line drawn in the Atlantic later gave Portugal the eastern part of South America, which became Brazil.

society.text: The Medici are driven out of Florence after the French king, Charles VIII, invades Italy, and the preacher Savonarola gains power.
society.context: The Medici were expelled in November. They did not return to rule the city until 1512.

technology.text: The Italian mathematician Luca Pacioli publishes a textbook describing double-entry bookkeeping, the basis of modern accounting.
technology.context: The book, Summa de arithmetica, was printed in Venice. Merchants had used the method for a long time, but this was the first full printed account.

arts_culture.text: The Venetian printer Aldus Manutius sets up his press in Venice, and soon produces elegant, pocket-sized editions of the classics.
arts_culture.context: He started around this time. He later introduced italic type.

politics.text: Louis XII becomes king of France after Charles VIII dies from hitting his head on a low doorway.
politics.context: Charles died in April. Louis went on to claim Milan, continuing France's wars in Italy.

society.text: The preacher Girolamo Savonarola is hanged and burned in the main square of Florence after losing the city's support.
society.context: He was executed in May. Two years before, he had led the "bonfire of the vanities".

technology.text: The Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut, in India, by sailing round Africa.
technology.context: He arrived in May. It opened a direct sea route from Europe to Asia and made Portugal rich.

arts_culture.text: Leonardo da Vinci completes The Last Supper, on the wall of a dining hall in Milan.
arts_culture.context: He finished it around this year. Because he used experimental paint, it began to flake within his lifetime.

arts_culture.text: The German artist Albrecht Dürer publishes The Apocalypse, a series of woodcuts showing scenes from the Book of Revelation.
arts_culture.context: The prints made the young Dürer famous across Europe.

politics.text: Spanish adventurers led by Hernán Cortés are received by Aztec emperor Moctezuma II at his capital, Tenochtitlan.
politics.context: The meeting took place in November. Within two years Cortés had destroyed the Aztec empire.

politics.text: Charles of Habsburg, king of Spain, is elected Holy Roman Emperor as Charles V, beating King Francis I of France to the crown.
politics.context: He was elected in June after a costly campaign of bribes. The rivalry between the two kings shaped European wars for decades.

society.text: The Swiss priest Huldrych Zwingli begins preaching straight from the Gospels in Zurich, breaking with church custom.
society.context: He started at the Grossmünster on New Year's Day, launching the Swiss Reformation.

society.text: Hernán Cortés founds the town of Veracruz on the Mexican coast, the first Spanish settlement on the mainland of New Spain.
society.context: He founded it in April, then scuttled his ships to stop his men from turning back.

technology.text: Five ships under the Portuguese captain Ferdinand Magellan leave Seville on the first voyage to sail around the world.
technology.context: Magellan died on the way. The Spanish navigator Elcano brought the survivors home in 1522.

arts_culture.text: The Italian painter and inventor Leonardo da Vinci dies at Amboise, in France, as a guest of King Francis I.
arts_culture.context: He died in May, aged 67. He had brought the Mona Lisa with him, which is why it now hangs in the Louvre.

arts_culture.text: King Francis I of France orders the building of the Château de Chambord, a vast hunting lodge in the Loire valley.
arts_culture.context: Work began in September. The château has a famous double-spiral staircase, traditionally linked to Leonardo da Vinci.

politics.text: Hernán Cortés and his native allies capture Tenochtitlan after a long siege, ending the Aztec empire.
politics.context: The city fell in August. It became the site of Mexico City.

politics.text: The Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent captures the fortress of Belgrade, opening the way into Hungary.
politics.context: Belgrade fell in August. It opened Hungary to the Ottomans, who crushed the Hungarian army at Mohács five years later.

society.text: The German monk Martin Luther refuses to retract his writings before Emperor Charles V and is declared an outlaw.
society.context: He appeared at the Diet of Worms in April. The Edict of Worms followed in May.

technology.text: Ferdinand Magellan's Spanish-sponsored fleet reaches the Philippines, named later for King Philip of Spain.
technology.context: Magellan reached the islands in March and was killed in a fight there a month later. His surviving crew, under Elcano, completed the first voyage round the world.

arts_culture.text: The Franco-Flemish composer Josquin des Prez, the most admired musician of his age, dies in Condé-sur-l'Escaut.
arts_culture.context: He died in August. Martin Luther praised him as the master of the notes.

politics.text: Suleiman the Magnificent's Ottoman army crushes the Hungarians at Mohács, and King Louis II dies fleeing the field.
politics.context: The battle took only about two hours. Hungary fell apart, and the Ottomans held much of it for about a century and a half.

politics.text: Francis I of France signs the Treaty of Madrid, after being held prisoner by Emperor Charles V.
politics.context: Francis was captured at the Battle of Pavia the year before. Once free, he broke the treaty.

society.text: Muslims in Aragon and Catalonia face a deadline to be baptised as Christians or leave Spain.
society.context: Muslims in Castile had already been forced to convert. Those who converted were called Moriscos, and were watched closely.

technology.text: At Panipat, Babur's cannon and matchlock guns, new to northern India, shatter the army of the Sultan of Delhi and begin the Mughal Empire.
technology.context: Babur was a prince from Central Asia. His army's firepower beat a far larger force with war elephants. His family ruled India until the nineteenth century.

arts_culture.text: William Tyndale's English translation of the New Testament, printed abroad, begins to reach England.
arts_culture.context: It was smuggled in and banned. Bishop Tunstall had copies burned in London in October. Tyndale was later executed for his work.

politics.text: Portuguese sailors blown off course land on Tanegashima, in Japan, and introduce the first firearms to the country.
politics.context: Japanese smiths copied the guns within a few years.

society.text: King Henry VIII of England marries his sixth and last wife, Catherine Parr, at Hampton Court.
society.context: She had been widowed twice before, and she wrote books under her own name. Henry died in 1547, and she outlived him.

technology.text: The Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus publishes his theory that the Earth orbits the Sun, as he lies dying.
technology.context: The book was De revolutionibus. He is said to have seen a printed copy on his deathbed.

technology.text: The Flemish anatomist Andreas Vesalius publishes On the Fabric of the Human Body, a landmark of anatomy, in Basel.
technology.context: The book was based on his own dissections and corrected centuries-old errors.

arts_culture.text: The German painter Hans Holbein the Younger, court artist to King Henry VIII, dies in London.
arts_culture.context: Holbein is best known for his portraits of Henry VIII's court, such as The Ambassadors. He probably died of plague in the autumn.

politics.text: A Holy League fleet of Spanish, Venetian and papal ships destroys the Ottoman navy at the Battle of Lepanto, off Greece.
politics.context: It was the largest sea battle in the Mediterranean for centuries, fought mostly by galleys. The writer Miguel de Cervantes was wounded there and lost the use of his left hand.

politics.text: The Ottomans take Famagusta, ending their conquest of Cyprus from Venice.
politics.context: The siege had lasted for months. Cyprus stayed in Ottoman hands for about three centuries.

society.text: Crimean Tatar raiders burn most of Moscow, killing many people, while Ivan the Terrible's government is caught unprepared.
society.context: The fire spread fast through the city's wooden buildings. Ivan fled before the raiders arrived. Moscow was rebuilt.

society.text: Queen Elizabeth the First founds Jesus College at Oxford, which will educate many Welsh students.
society.context: The college was founded by a Welshman, Hugh Price. T. E. Lawrence, known as Lawrence of Arabia, studied there centuries later.

technology.text: The German astronomer Johannes Kepler, who will discover how the planets move, is born in Weil der Stadt.
technology.context: His three laws showed the planets moving in ellipses, and helped Newton. He worked for Tycho Brahe and the Emperor Rudolf the Second.

arts_culture.text: The painter Caravaggio, a master of dramatic light and shadow, is born in Milan.
arts_culture.context: He led a violent life, and fled Rome after killing a man in 1606. His style influenced painters across Europe.

arts_culture.text: Queen Elizabeth the First opens London's Royal Exchange, a grand centre for merchants built by Thomas Gresham.
arts_culture.context: Gresham, a rich merchant, paid for the building. It was later destroyed in the Great Fire of London.

politics.text: The Spanish execute Túpac Amaru, the last ruler of the Inca state at Vilcabamba, in the main square of Cusco.
politics.context: He was captured in the summer and executed in September. His death ended the last Inca resistance to Spanish rule.

society.text: Catholic mobs in Paris murder thousands of Protestant Huguenots in the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre.
society.context: The killings began in Paris in August, days after a royal wedding, and spread to other French cities. They deepened the wars of religion in France.

technology.text: The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe observes a brilliant new star in the constellation Cassiopeia.
technology.context: He saw it in November. It was a supernova, and it challenged the idea of an unchanging sky.

arts_culture.text: The Portuguese poet Luís de Camões publishes The Lusiads, an epic poem about Vasco da Gama's voyage to India.
arts_culture.context: It was published in Lisbon.

politics.text: The Japanese warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi sends a huge army across the sea to invade Korea, beginning the Imjin War.
politics.context: The first landings were in April. The war, with a pause, lasted until 1598. Korea, helped by Ming China, finally drove the Japanese out.

society.text: Plague closes London's theatres, leaving actors and playwrights without work.
society.context: Thousands of Londoners died, and the theatres stayed shut for much of the next two years. Shakespeare wrote the poem Venus and Adonis in this time.

technology.text: The Korean admiral Yi Sun-sin destroys a Japanese fleet with his armoured turtle ships at the Battle of Hansando.
technology.context: Yi's victory in August cut Japanese supply lines by sea and helped save Korea from conquest.

arts_culture.text: A pamphlet by the writer Robert Greene attacks an "upstart crow", the first known mention of William Shakespeare as a London playwright.
arts_culture.context: Greene wrote it as he lay dying, in the early autumn. The "upstart crow" is usually taken to mean Shakespeare, who was then making his name.

politics.text: Tokugawa Ieyasu defeats rival warlords at the Battle of Sekigahara, in Japan, clearing his path to become shogun.
politics.context: It was fought in October. He took the title of shogun three years later.

society.text: Queen Elizabeth I grants a royal charter to the English East India Company, a trading firm that will come to rule much of India.
society.context: The charter, granted on the last day of the year, gave the company a monopoly on English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope.

society.text: The Italian philosopher Giordano Bruno is burned at the stake in Rome for heresy.
society.context: He was burned in February in the Campo de' Fiori. Among other things, he had argued that the stars were distant suns.

technology.text: The English physician William Gilbert publishes De Magnete, arguing that the Earth itself is a giant magnet.
technology.context: Gilbert was physician to Queen Elizabeth I.

arts_culture.text: The Italian composer Jacopo Peri's Euridice, the earliest opera that survives, is first performed in Florence.
arts_culture.context: It was staged in October, at the wedding of Maria de' Medici and King Henry IV of France.

politics.text: Akbar, the great Mughal emperor of India, dies at Agra, and his son Jahangir takes the throne.
politics.context: Akbar built the Mughal Empire into a vast and fairly tolerant state. He died in October, and his son Jahangir succeeded him.

society.text: English Catholics led by Guy Fawkes are foiled in a plot to blow up King James I and Parliament in London.
society.context: Fawkes was caught guarding barrels of gunpowder beneath the Parliament building in November.

technology.text: The printer Johann Carolus begins publishing a weekly newsletter in Strasbourg, often called the first newspaper.
technology.context: The weekly was called Relation. It is usually counted as the first printed newspaper.

arts_culture.text: The Spanish writer Miguel de Cervantes publishes the first part of Don Quixote, a novel about a deluded knight.
arts_culture.context: The first part appeared in Madrid in January and was an instant success. Don Quixote is often called the first modern novel.

politics.text: Japan's Satsuma clan invades the Ryukyu Kingdom and takes its king prisoner.
politics.context: The invasion began in the spring. The kingdom, on Okinawa, became a vassal of Satsuma.

politics.text: Spain and the Dutch Republic agree the Twelve Years' Truce, pausing a long war.
politics.context: The truce, signed in April, paused the Dutch war of independence from Spain and helped the Dutch Republic grow into a major trading power.

society.text: The English explorer Henry Hudson, sailing for the Dutch, enters the North American river that will bear his name.
society.context: He sailed up the river in September, looking for a route to Asia. His voyage gave the Dutch their claim to the land that became New Amsterdam.

technology.text: The Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei builds a telescope in Venice and turns it on the Moon, seeing mountains and craters.
technology.context: He built it in August, after hearing of a Dutch invention, and began studying the Moon in the autumn.

arts_culture.text: William Shakespeare's Sonnets are published in London, probably without his permission.
arts_culture.context: The book contained 154 sonnets and was printed by Thomas Thorpe.

politics.text: King Henry IV of France is stabbed to death in his carriage in Paris by a Catholic fanatic, François Ravaillac.
politics.context: The king was killed in May. He had ended France's wars of religion with the Edict of Nantes in 1598.

society.text: Spanish settlers found Santa Fe, in what is now New Mexico, one of the oldest European towns in the United States.
society.context: Pedro de Peralta founded it as the colony's capital.

technology.text: The Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei discovers four moons orbiting Jupiter and publishes the news in The Starry Messenger.
technology.context: He first saw them in January. The discovery showed that not everything in the sky circles the Earth, which weakened the old view of the universe.

arts_culture.text: The Italian painter Caravaggio, famous for his dramatic light and shadow, dies on the Tuscan coast while travelling to Rome.
arts_culture.context: Caravaggio died in July, at about thirty-eight, on his way to Rome to seek a pardon for a killing.

politics.text: King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden is killed leading a cavalry charge at the Battle of Lützen, in the Thirty Years' War.
politics.context: He died in November, though his army won the battle. His death was a heavy blow to the Protestant cause in the war.

society.text: Swedish rulers found the University of Tartu, in what is now Estonia.
society.context: It was founded in June, as the Academia Gustaviana. Estonia was then part of the Swedish empire.

technology.text: The Italian scientist Galileo Galilei publishes his Dialogue about the two chief world systems, defending a Sun-centred universe.
technology.context: It led to his trial for heresy the following year.

arts_culture.text: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan begins building the Taj Mahal, at Agra, as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
arts_culture.context: Work began soon after her death the year before.

politics.text: Christian peasants rise against heavy taxes at Shimabara, in Japan, in a revolt the shogunate will crush the next year.
politics.context: The Shimabara Rebellion began late in the year and was crushed in 1638. The shogunate then banned Christianity and closed Japan to most foreigners.

society.text: Tulip prices collapse in the Dutch Republic, ending a speculative frenzy among traders in Amsterdam and Haarlem.
society.context: Tulip mania peaked over the winter and crashed in February. Historians now debate how widespread it was.

technology.text: The French philosopher René Descartes publishes Discourse on Method, setting out his approach to scientific reasoning.
technology.context: It was printed in Leiden, in the Dutch Republic, in June, and appeared without his name. It was written in French, not Latin, so that ordinary readers could follow it.

arts_culture.text: The French playwright Pierre Corneille's tragicomedy Le Cid premieres in Paris and sparks a bitter literary quarrel.
arts_culture.context: It opened at the very start of the year. The exact date is uncertain.

politics.text: King Charles I raises his standard at Nottingham, and civil war breaks out between his supporters and Parliament.
politics.context: Charles raised his flag in August after Parliament refused to obey him. The war ended with his defeat and, in 1649, his execution.

society.text: The Dutch navigator Abel Tasman becomes the first European to sight the island later named Tasmania.
society.context: He sighted it in November, and went on to find New Zealand. He named the island Van Diemen's Land.

technology.text: The French teenager Blaise Pascal invents a mechanical calculator to help his tax-collector father.
technology.context: He began work on the Pascaline this year, at the age of eighteen. It could add and subtract by turning dials.

arts_culture.text: The Dutch painter Rembrandt completes The Night Watch, a huge group portrait of an Amsterdam militia company.
arts_culture.context: The nickname came later, because dark varnish made the scene look like night. The real title is The Militia Company of District II. It now hangs in the Rijksmuseum.

politics.text: Treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück end the Thirty Years' War and reshape the borders of the Holy Roman Empire.
politics.context: The Peace of Westphalia was agreed in October. It ended thirty years of war and is often seen as the start of the modern system of independent states.

society.text: Cossacks led by Bohdan Khmelnytsky rise against Polish nobles in what is now Ukraine.
society.context: The uprising began in the spring and led to a Cossack state. It weakened Poland-Lithuania and reshaped eastern Europe.

technology.text: The Cossack explorer Semyon Dezhnev sails round the north-eastern tip of Asia, through the strait later named after Bering.
technology.context: Almost nobody heard of the voyage for decades.

technology.text: At Blaise Pascal's request, his brother-in-law carries a barometer up the Puy de Dôme, showing that air pressure falls with height.
technology.context: The experiment, in September, helped show that air has weight. The unit of pressure, the pascal, is named after him.

arts_culture.text: The white marble mausoleum built by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal is completed at Agra.
arts_culture.context: This is the main tomb of the Taj Mahal. The wider complex took several more years.

arts_culture.text: The Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture is founded in Paris, as a school for the king's artists.
arts_culture.context: It was founded in January and became a model for national art academies across Europe.

politics.text: At the Battle of Warsaw, a Swedish and Brandenburg army beats the Polish-Lithuanian forces in a three-day fight.
politics.context: It was part of a war that Poles call the Deluge. King Charles X Gustav of Sweden led the allied army.

politics.text: London's Lord Mayor suggests that Oliver Cromwell take the crown, but Cromwell turns it down.
politics.context: Cromwell ruled England as Lord Protector. He was offered the crown again the next year, and he refused again.

society.text: The English Parliament convicts the Quaker James Nayler of blasphemy but spares his life, after his followers greeted him like Christ.
society.context: Nayler had ridden into Bristol while his followers sang his praises. He was flogged and branded instead. The case showed how afraid many were of radical sects.

technology.text: The Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens invents the pendulum clock, which keeps far better time than any clock before it.
technology.context: He invented it on Christmas Day and patented it the following year. Pendulum clocks stayed the most accurate timekeepers for almost three hundred years.

arts_culture.text: Diego Velázquez paints Las Meninas, a royal portrait of the Spanish court in which the painter himself stands at his easel.
arts_culture.context: It shows the young Infanta Margarita with her maids and attendants in the palace. It is one of the most studied paintings in Western art.

arts_culture.text: King John Casimir of Poland crowns the Black Madonna of Częstochowa as Queen and Protector of Poland.
arts_culture.context: The crowning took place in Lwów, in April. The icon is still Poland's most revered holy image.

politics.text: The Maratha leader Shivaji escapes from house arrest at Emperor Aurangzeb's court in Agra, reputedly in a basket of sweets.
politics.context: He slipped away in August and went on to found the Maratha Empire, which later took on the Mughals.

society.text: A fire that starts in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane destroys most of the City of London.
society.context: The Great Fire burned for four days in September. It destroyed about thirteen thousand houses and St Paul's Cathedral, though few deaths were recorded.

technology.text: King Louis XIV's minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert founds the Académie des sciences in Paris.
technology.context: It was set up in December as a centre of French science, with the king's support.

arts_culture.text: The French playwright Molière's comedy The Misanthrope, about a man who hates hypocrisy, opens in Paris.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in June at the Palais-Royal theatre. It was not a great success at first, but is now one of Molière's best-loved plays.

arts_culture.text: The Dutch painter Frans Hals, famous for his lively portraits, dies in Haarlem.
arts_culture.context: He died in August. Hals was famous for loose-brushed, laughing portraits such as The Laughing Cavalier.

politics.text: The Qing navy under Admiral Shi Lang defeats the Zheng regime and takes Taiwan for China.
politics.context: The Zheng family had held the island since driving out the Dutch in 1662. Taiwan then came under Qing rule for two centuries.

politics.text: A relief army led by King Jan III Sobieski of Poland routs the Ottoman besiegers of Vienna.
politics.context: The Battle of Vienna, in September, ended the Ottoman siege and began the empire's long retreat from central Europe.

society.text: The Ashmolean Museum opens in Oxford, the first university museum in the world.
society.context: It opened in May, built around the collection of Elias Ashmole. Its treasures included a stuffed dodo.

technology.text: The Dutch microscopist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek describes tiny living creatures, later called bacteria, scraped from teeth.
technology.context: He described them in a letter to the Royal Society in September. His handmade single-lens microscopes magnified up to about 270 times.

arts_culture.text: The English composer Henry Purcell writes an ode for the feast of Saint Cecilia, patron saint of music, in London.
arts_culture.context: The ode was Welcome to All the Pleasures. It was first performed in November.

politics.text: The Ottoman army is crushed at the Second Battle of Mohács, in Hungary, by the forces of the Holy Roman Empire.
politics.context: The battle, in August, was a heavy defeat for the Ottomans. It helped the Habsburgs take control of Hungary.

society.text: A Venetian shell hits an Ottoman gunpowder store inside the Parthenon, in Athens, and blows the roof off the ancient temple.
society.context: The explosion, in September, destroyed much of the roof and many sculptures of a building that had stood almost intact for over two thousand years.

technology.text: The English scientist Isaac Newton publishes the Principia, setting out his laws of motion and universal gravitation.
technology.context: It was published in July. Its laws explained both falling apples and orbiting planets, and shaped physics for over two centuries.

arts_culture.text: The Italian-born French composer Jean-Baptiste Lully dies in Paris after striking his foot with his conducting staff.
arts_culture.context: He died in March, of gangrene, after hitting his foot with his staff while conducting a Te Deum. He had been court composer to Louis XIV.

politics.text: George Louis succeeds his father as Elector of Hanover. He will later become King George the First of Great Britain.
politics.context: He became king in 1714, the first of the House of Hanover. He was elector from January.

politics.text: The Russian Streltsy, a corps of rebel musketeers, face mass executions after a failed uprising against Peter the Great.
politics.context: Peter was abroad on his tour of Europe when the revolt began. He hurried home and had the leaders put to death, many in public.

society.text: Tsar Peter the Great imposes a tax on beards, to push Russian nobles to look more like Western Europeans.
society.context: Peter had just come back from touring Western Europe. People who paid the tax got a token to show it. Many Russians saw beards as a sign of faith.

society.text: Scottish settlers sail from Leith to found a colony at Darien in Panama, in a scheme backed by much of Scotland's wealth.
society.context: The Darien scheme collapsed within two years, through disease, hunger and Spanish hostility. Its failure helped push Scotland towards union with England.

technology.text: The English engineer Thomas Savery patents a steam-powered pump to drain flooded mines.
technology.context: It had no piston and could be dangerous, but it used the power of steam. Thomas Newcomen later improved on it.

technology.text: The world's first open-sea lighthouse is lit on the Eddystone Rocks off Plymouth, a reef where ships had been wrecked for centuries.
technology.context: Its builder, Henry Winstanley, made it of wood and stone. A great storm swept it away a few years later, and Winstanley died with it.

arts_culture.text: The English clergyman Jeremy Collier publishes a fierce attack on the immorality of the English stage.
arts_culture.context: His pamphlet, A Short View, hit playwrights such as Congreve and Vanbrugh. It helped push the theatre towards milder comedy.

politics.text: Aurangzeb, the last great Mughal emperor, dies in Ahmednagar, and his empire begins to fall apart.
politics.context: He died in March after almost fifty years on the throne. His long wars drained the empire, which declined after his death.

politics.text: England and Scotland unite as the Kingdom of Great Britain under the Acts of Union.
politics.context: The Union took effect on the first of May. It created a single parliament at Westminster and ended Scotland's separate parliament.

society.text: A huge earthquake shakes Japan, and weeks later Mount Fuji erupts for the last time in recorded history.
society.context: The Hōei earthquake in October, and its tsunami, killed thousands. Fuji erupted in December, and ash fell on Edo (now Tokyo), about a hundred kilometres away.

technology.text: The French physicist Denis Papin sails a small steam-driven paddle boat on the River Fulda, in Germany.
technology.context: Local boatmen are said to have smashed the boat soon afterwards.

arts_culture.text: The Danish-German organist Dieterich Buxtehude, whom the young Bach once walked miles to hear, dies in Lübeck.
arts_culture.context: He died in May. Bach had visited him two years earlier.

politics.text: Diplomats gather at Utrecht, in the Dutch Republic, to negotiate an end to the War of the Spanish Succession.
politics.context: The congress opened in January. It led to the Peace of Utrecht the next year, which ended the war and shifted the balance of power in Europe.

society.text: A court in Hertfordshire convicts Jane Wenham of witchcraft, the last such conviction in England.
society.context: The judge secured her pardon soon afterwards.

technology.text: The English inventor Thomas Newcomen installs the first practical steam engine, to pump water out of a coal mine near Dudley.
technology.context: It was installed at the Conygree coalworks.

arts_culture.text: The English poet Alexander Pope publishes the first version of The Rape of the Lock, a mock-heroic poem about a stolen curl of hair.
arts_culture.context: The first version, in two cantos, appeared in May. Pope wrote it to settle a quarrel between two families over a cut lock of hair, and expanded it two years later.

politics.text: Robert Walpole becomes the chief minister of Britain's government, and is later seen as the first prime minister.
politics.context: Walpole held power for more than twenty years. The title "prime minister" was at first meant as an insult.

politics.text: Peter the Great is proclaimed Emperor of All the Russias, after winning the long Great Northern War against Sweden.
politics.context: The peace treaty of Nystad ended the war. Peter had ruled Russia as tsar for decades.

society.text: James Franklin starts the New-England Courant in Boston, a paper that mocks the authorities, and his young brother Benjamin works for it.
society.context: Benjamin Franklin was an apprentice in the printing shop. He later secretly wrote letters for the paper under the name Silence Dogood.

technology.text: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu has her young daughter inoculated against smallpox in London, after seeing the method used in Turkey.
technology.context: She had seen the practice in Constantinople, where her husband was ambassador. Royal doctors watched the test, and the method became fashionable at court.

arts_culture.text: Johann Sebastian Bach sends the Margrave of Brandenburg six concertos, now known as the Brandenburg Concertos.
arts_culture.context: Bach dedicated the music in March. The Margrave may never have had them played, and the music was nearly forgotten until the nineteenth century.

politics.text: The Persian ruler Nader Shah sacks Delhi, taking the Peacock Throne and vast treasure from the Mughal Empire.
politics.context: He took the city in March and ordered a massacre of its people. The raid left the Mughal Empire badly weakened.

society.text: Enslaved people rise in the Stono Rebellion near Charleston, South Carolina, the largest slave revolt in the British mainland colonies.
society.context: It began in September when about twenty enslaved people seized weapons. It was put down, and South Carolina passed harsher slave laws.

technology.text: The French engineer Jacques de Vaucanson shows a mechanical duck that appears to eat, digest and excrete grain.
technology.context: He showed it in Paris.

arts_culture.text: George Frideric Handel's oratorio Israel in Egypt is first performed in London.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in April and was poorly received at first, because audiences found its choruses too heavy.

politics.text: Bonnie Prince Charlie raises his standard at Glenfinnan in Scotland, starting a Jacobite rising to win back the British throne.
politics.context: The prince was the grandson of James II. His highland army marched into England as far as Derby before turning back.

society.text: Madame de Pompadour is presented at the French court and soon becomes the official mistress of King Louis the Fifteenth.
society.context: She was the daughter of a financier. She became a patron of artists and writers such as Voltaire, and had great influence over the king.

technology.text: A German priest, Ewald von Kleist, discovers how to store electric charge in a glass jar, an invention later called the Leyden jar.
technology.context: The Dutch scientist Pieter van Musschenbroek made the same discovery in Leiden at about the same time, and the jar is named after his city.

technology.text: The Italian scientist Alessandro Volta, who will invent the electric battery, is born in Como.
technology.context: The unit of electric potential, the volt, is named after him.

arts_culture.text: The Irish writer Jonathan Swift, author of Gulliver's Travels, dies in Dublin.
arts_culture.context: Swift was also dean of St Patrick's Cathedral. He left most of his money to found a hospital for the mentally ill.

politics.text: General Edward Braddock's British army is ambushed and routed by French and Native American forces near the Monongahela River.
politics.context: Braddock was marching to attack Fort Duquesne. The defeat, in July, was an early disaster for Britain in the French and Indian War.

society.text: A huge earthquake, tsunami and fire destroy much of Lisbon, the Portuguese capital, on All Saints' Day.
society.context: It struck on the first of November, while many people were at church, and killed tens of thousands. It shook beliefs about divine order across Europe.

technology.text: The German philosopher Immanuel Kant proposes that the solar system formed from a spinning cloud of gas and dust.
technology.context: He published the idea anonymously.

arts_culture.text: The English writer Samuel Johnson publishes A Dictionary of the English Language, after nearly nine years of work.
arts_culture.context: It was published in April. It was the leading English dictionary for over a century, and Johnson wrote it with only a few assistants.

politics.text: Hyder Ali of Mysore dictates peace terms to the British outside Madras, ending the First Anglo-Mysore War.
politics.context: Hyder Ali had won a string of victories and forced the British to sign the Treaty of Madras in April, in the First Anglo-Mysore War.

society.text: The Spanish Franciscan friar Junípero Serra founds Mission San Diego, the first of the California missions.
society.context: He founded it in July. It was the first of twenty-one missions along the California coast, several of which grew into cities.

technology.text: The Scottish engineer James Watt patents a steam engine with a separate condenser, far more efficient than earlier engines.
technology.context: The patent was granted in January. Watt's engines later powered factories and mines in the Industrial Revolution.

technology.text: Captain James Cook observes the transit of Venus from Tahiti, before sailing on to chart the coast of New Zealand.
technology.context: He observed the transit in June on his first voyage in the Endeavour. Such observations helped scientists work out the distance from the Earth to the Sun.

arts_culture.text: The Royal Academy of Arts, with Joshua Reynolds as its first president, holds its first exhibition in London.
arts_culture.context: King George III backed the Academy, to train artists and show their work. Its yearly Summer Exhibition began this year and is still held today.

politics.text: After crossing the icy Delaware River at night, George Washington's army surprises and defeats a Hessian garrison at Trenton, New Jersey.
politics.context: The victory lifted American hopes during a grim winter. Hessians were German soldiers hired by Britain.

society.text: The Scottish thinker Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations, a book that argues for free markets.
society.context: The book explained how the division of labour and competition could make nations richer. It became the founding work of modern economics.

technology.text: James Watt and his partner Matthew Boulton sell their improved steam engines to customers for the first time.
technology.context: Watt's engine used far less coal than earlier engines. It helped power the Industrial Revolution.

technology.text: Captain James Cook sets sail from Plymouth on a third voyage of exploration, which will end with his death in Hawaii.
technology.context: He sailed in July. He was killed in a clash with islanders at Kealakekua Bay.

arts_culture.text: The historian Edward Gibbon publishes the first volume of his Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, which sells out within weeks.
arts_culture.context: Gibbon took more than a decade to finish all the volumes. His elegant, ironic style made the work famous.

politics.text: A British army under Lord Cornwallis surrenders to American and French forces at Yorktown, Virginia.
politics.context: The surrender, in October, effectively ended the fighting in the American Revolutionary War and led to peace talks with Britain.

society.text: The Austrian emperor Joseph II grants Protestants and Orthodox Christians the right to worship in his lands.
society.context: He issued the Patent of Toleration in October as part of his reforms. Similar rights for Jews followed soon afterwards.

technology.text: The British astronomer William Herschel discovers a new planet, Uranus, using a telescope he built himself, in Bath.
technology.context: He found it in March and at first thought it was a comet. It was the first planet discovered with a telescope.

arts_culture.text: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's opera Idomeneo premieres in Munich.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in January at the court theatre in Munich. It is Mozart's first great serious opera, about a king of Crete.

politics.text: Thomas Jefferson is appointed the first Secretary of State of the United States, by President George Washington.
politics.context: He was then the American minister in Paris. He returned home and took up the job soon afterwards.

society.text: Thousands of Parisian women march to Versailles in the rain over the price of bread, and force the king to return to Paris.
society.context: The march was in October. The royal family was then kept in Paris under the eye of the crowds.

technology.text: The French chemist Antoine Lavoisier publishes his Elementary Treatise on Chemistry, setting out the modern idea of chemical elements.
technology.context: It included the first modern list of the elements and helped overturn the old theory of phlogiston. He was guillotined five years later.

arts_culture.text: Olaudah Equiano, a former slave, publishes his life story in London, a bestseller that helps the campaign against the slave trade.
arts_culture.context: He described his capture in West Africa and his life at sea. The book was reprinted many times.

politics.text: Enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue launch a revolt that grows into the Haitian Revolution.
politics.context: It began in August in the north of the island. It led to the end of slavery in the colony and, in 1804, to Haiti's independence.

politics.text: King Louis XVI and his family are caught at Varennes while trying to flee revolutionary Paris.
politics.context: The flight to Varennes was in June. It failed when the king was recognised, and it destroyed trust in him before his overthrow the next year.

society.text: The young United States ratifies the Bill of Rights, ten amendments protecting individual freedoms.
society.context: The ratification was completed in December. The amendments guarantee freedoms such as speech, religion and a fair trial.

technology.text: The Italian scientist Luigi Galvani publishes his findings on electricity in the muscles of frogs.
technology.context: His work on "animal electricity" led Alessandro Volta to build the first battery.

arts_culture.text: Austrian composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's fairy-tale opera The Magic Flute premieres in a suburban theatre in Vienna.
arts_culture.context: The librettist, Emanuel Schikaneder, ran the theatre and played the bird-catcher Papageno. Mozart died just over two months after the opening.

politics.text: Revolutionary France wins its first great victory at Valmy, and the National Convention declares France a republic.
politics.context: Valmy was fought on the twentieth of September, and the republic was declared the next day. The victory saved the Revolution from invasion.

society.text: The English writer Mary Wollstonecraft publishes A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, arguing that women deserve an education.
society.context: It came out in January and argued that girls deserve the same education as boys. It is seen as an early work of feminist thought.

technology.text: The Scottish engineer William Murdoch lights his house in Redruth, in Cornwall, with gas made from coal.
technology.context: He lit the house in the early part of the 1790s. Gas lighting later spread to factories and city streets.

arts_culture.text: A French army officer, Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle, writes a marching song in Strasbourg that becomes the French national anthem.
arts_culture.context: He wrote it in April as a war song for the Army of the Rhine. It was named after the volunteers from Marseille who sang it as they marched into Paris.

politics.text: King Louis XVI of France is executed by guillotine in Paris.
politics.context: He was executed in January after being found guilty of treason. His death horrified Europe's monarchies, and Britain and Spain soon went to war with France.

society.text: The Committee of Public Safety begins the Reign of Terror in France, as thousands go to the guillotine.
society.context: It was declared in September. Over the next year many thousands were executed, including Queen Marie Antoinette.

technology.text: The American inventor Eli Whitney builds a machine that quickly separates cotton fibres from their seeds, the cotton gin.
technology.context: He built it in Georgia and patented it the next year.

arts_culture.text: The French painter Jacques-Louis David completes The Death of Marat, showing the murdered revolutionary in his bath.
arts_culture.context: David painted it in the months after Marat was murdered in July by Charlotte Corday. It turned the dead journalist into a martyr of the Revolution.

politics.text: Napoleon Bonaparte lands a French army in Egypt, hoping to threaten British India.
politics.context: He landed in July and won the Battle of the Pyramids. Nelson soon destroyed the French fleet, leaving the army stranded in Egypt.

politics.text: Admiral Horatio Nelson destroys the French fleet at the Battle of the Nile, in Aboukir Bay, off Egypt.
politics.context: The battle was fought in early August, cutting off Napoleon's army in Egypt.

society.text: The English clergyman Thomas Malthus publishes An Essay on the Principle of Population, warning that people will outrun food.
society.context: It first appeared anonymously.

technology.text: The English doctor Edward Jenner publishes his study showing that cowpox inoculation protects against smallpox.
technology.context: He had tested the idea on a boy, James Phipps, two years earlier.

arts_culture.text: The English poets William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge publish Lyrical Ballads, a landmark of Romanticism.
arts_culture.context: It appeared anonymously in the autumn. Critics were cool at first, but the book's plain language became a landmark of English Romantic poetry.

politics.text: British forces storm Seringapatam, in southern India, and kill Tipu Sultan, the ruler of Mysore.
politics.context: The city fell in May, ending the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War. Britain's victory left it the strongest power in southern India.

politics.text: Napoleon Bonaparte seizes power in a coup in Paris and becomes First Consul of France.
politics.context: The coup took place in November. It overthrew the Directory, and Napoleon ruled France for the next fifteen years.

society.text: The German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt sets sail from Spain on a five-year scientific expedition to Latin America.
society.context: He left A Coruña in June with the botanist Aimé Bonpland. The expedition's maps and measurements gave Europe its first scientific picture of the region.

technology.text: French soldiers digging a fort near Rashid, in Egypt, uncover a stone carved in three scripts that will unlock hieroglyphs.
technology.context: The Rosetta Stone was found in July. Its text in Greek and Egyptian scripts later let Jean-François Champollion decipher hieroglyphs.

arts_culture.text: Ludwig van Beethoven publishes his Pathétique piano sonata in Vienna.
arts_culture.context: Beethoven was in his late twenties. The sonata was a hit and helped make his name as a leading composer.

politics.text: Napoleon Bonaparte's army defeats the Austrians at the Battle of Marengo, in northern Italy.
politics.context: Marengo, fought in June, restored French control of northern Italy. It strengthened Napoleon's grip on power as First Consul.

society.text: The United States Congress founds the Library of Congress, as a small collection for lawmakers in the new capital.
society.context: It was founded in April. It later grew into one of the largest libraries in the world.

technology.text: The Italian physicist Alessandro Volta announces the voltaic pile, the first electric battery.
technology.context: He announced it in a letter to the Royal Society in March. The pile gave the first steady electric current, and the volt is named after Volta.

arts_culture.text: Ludwig van Beethoven conducts the premiere of his first symphony in Vienna.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in April at the Burgtheater. Its daring opening chord, in the "wrong" key, startled some listeners.

politics.text: Jean-Jacques Dessalines declares Haiti independent, taking back its Indigenous Taíno name and forming the first free Black republic.
politics.context: Dessalines declared Haiti free on New Year's Day. It was the only successful slave revolt to create a new state, after a long war against France.

politics.text: Napoleon Bonaparte crowns himself Emperor of the French, in Notre-Dame cathedral in Paris.
politics.context: The coronation was in December. Pope Pius VII looked on.

politics.text: Lieutenant Stephen Decatur leads a night raid into Tripoli harbour and burns the captured American frigate Philadelphia.
