politics.context: It happened in February, during the First Barbary War. The Philadelphia had run aground and been taken, and Decatur burned her so that Tripoli could not use her.

society.text: The American explorers Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out up the Missouri River from St. Louis to find a route to the Pacific.
society.context: They left in May and reached the Pacific coast in 1805. President Jefferson sent them to map the lands of the Louisiana Purchase.

technology.text: Richard Trevithick's steam locomotive hauls iron and passengers along a tramway at Merthyr Tydfil, in Wales.
technology.context: It ran in February. It was the first steam locomotive to haul a load on rails, though the cast-iron track often broke under its weight.

arts_culture.text: The German dramatist Friedrich Schiller's play Wilhelm Tell, about a Swiss archer who defies a tyrant, is first staged in Weimar.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in March at the court theatre in Weimar. It was Schiller's last completed play, and the Swiss came to treat it as a national story.

politics.text: Portugal's royal court flees Napoleon's invading army and sails from Lisbon for Brazil, soon making Rio de Janeiro its capital.
politics.context: The court sailed in November, just ahead of French troops. It was the only time a European monarchy ruled from one of its colonies.

politics.text: The British navy bombards Copenhagen and seizes the Danish fleet, to stop it falling into Napoleon's hands.
politics.context: The attack in September stopped Napoleon from using the Danish fleet. It was controversial, as Denmark was neutral.

society.text: The British Parliament passes an act abolishing the slave trade throughout the British Empire.
society.context: The Slave Trade Act received royal assent in March. Slavery itself continued until later.

technology.text: The American inventor Robert Fulton's steamboat makes its first run up the Hudson River from New York City to Albany.
technology.context: The trip began in August and took about thirty-two hours. It showed that steamboats could be a commercial success.

arts_culture.text: The young English poet Lord Byron publishes his first book of verse, Hours of Idleness.
arts_culture.context: A harsh review of it provoked his satire English Bards and Scotch Reviewers.

politics.text: The Mexican priest Miguel Hidalgo rings his church bell at Dolores and calls on his parish to rise against Spanish rule.
politics.context: The Cry of Dolores came in September and began the Mexican War of Independence.

society.text: Munich celebrates the wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria with horse races and a huge public party that becomes a yearly tradition.
society.context: It was the first Oktoberfest, held in October for the wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig and Princess Therese. It was so popular that it was repeated every year.

technology.text: The French confectioner Nicolas Appert publishes his method of preserving food in sealed glass jars.
technology.context: He had won a prize from Napoleon's government for the method.

arts_culture.text: The Scottish writer Walter Scott publishes The Lady of the Lake, a romantic poem set in the Highlands, and it becomes a bestseller.
arts_culture.context: It came out in May and was a huge bestseller. It made the Trossachs, in the Scottish Highlands, a tourist destination.

politics.text: The United States declares war on Britain, beginning a three-year conflict over trade, impressment and expansion.
politics.context: Congress voted for war in June. The conflict is known by the year it began.

society.text: Fires burn much of Moscow as Napoleon's army occupies the Russian city.
society.context: The fires started in September, soon after the French entered the city. Napoleon found no supplies and left a month later, beginning his disastrous retreat.

technology.text: The Scottish engineer Henry Bell launches the paddle steamer Comet on the River Clyde, the first successful commercial steamboat in Europe.
technology.context: It began carrying passengers in August, between Glasgow and Greenock. Its success sparked a boom in steamboats on British rivers.

arts_culture.text: The German brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm publish the first volume of their collected fairy tales.
arts_culture.context: It came out in December. The brothers collected the stories from oral tradition, and the book includes Cinderella and Hansel and Gretel.

politics.text: General Andrew Jackson's American troops defeat a larger British force outside New Orleans, after a peace treaty is already signed.
politics.context: The battle was fought in January. News of the Treaty of Ghent had not yet arrived.

politics.text: Napoleon Bonaparte is defeated by the Duke of Wellington and Marshal Blücher at the Battle of Waterloo, in Belgium.
politics.context: The battle in June ended Napoleon's rule for good, and he was exiled to Saint Helena. It was fought south of Brussels.

politics.text: The Congress of Vienna ends, redrawing the map of Europe after the defeat of Napoleon.
politics.context: Its final act was signed in June. The great powers aimed to keep a balance of power and prevent another war like the Napoleonic Wars.

politics.text: A US fleet under Stephen Decatur forces the Dey of Algiers to end tribute payments, in the Second Barbary War.
politics.context: For years, European states and the United States had paid the Barbary states to leave their ships alone. A treaty was signed in the summer, and the fleet then moved on to Tunis and Tripoli.

society.text: Mount Tambora erupts on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, the most powerful eruption in recorded history.
society.context: It erupted in April. The following year was known as the "year without a summer".

technology.text: The English chemist Humphry Davy invents a safety lamp that will not ignite the gas in coal mines.
technology.context: It cut the number of deaths from firedamp explosions.

arts_culture.text: The English novelist Jane Austen publishes Emma, a comedy about a matchmaking young woman in a country village.
arts_culture.context: Austen dedicated it to the Prince Regent, who admired her books. The title page says 1816. She died in 1817, aged 41.

politics.text: José de San Martín declares Peru independent from Spain in Lima.
politics.context: He declared it in July. Spanish forces held out in the mountains for years.

politics.text: Greek rebels rise against Ottoman rule, beginning the Greek War of Independence.
politics.context: The revolt began in March. After a long war, and with help from Britain, France and Russia, Greece won its independence in 1830.

society.text: Free Black Americans, backed by the American Colonization Society, acquire land at Cape Mesurado to found the colony of Liberia.
society.context: The Society wanted to settle free Black Americans in Africa. Liberia's capital, Monrovia, was later named after the US president James Monroe, who supported it.

technology.text: The English scientist Michael Faraday builds the first device that turns electricity into continuous motion.
technology.context: It was a forerunner of the electric motor. He demonstrated it in the autumn.

arts_culture.text: The German composer Carl Maria von Weber's opera Der Freischütz premieres in Berlin and launches German Romantic opera.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in June at the Schauspielhaus in Berlin and was an instant success. Its forest setting and magic became a model for Romantic opera.

politics.text: Patriots known as the Thirty-Three Orientals declare independence for the territory of Uruguay from Brazil.
politics.context: The declaration was in August. Brazil resisted, and the war that followed ended in 1828 with an independent Uruguay.

society.text: The Erie Canal opens, linking the Hudson River to the Great Lakes across New York State.
society.context: It opened in October, with cannon fired along its length. The canal made New York the leading port of the United States.

technology.text: The Stockton and Darlington Railway opens in northern England, the first public railway to use steam locomotives.
technology.context: George Stephenson's engine pulled the first train in September. The line carried coal first and passengers soon afterwards, and it inspired the railway age.

arts_culture.text: The French lawyer Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin publishes The Physiology of Taste, a famous book about food and dining.
arts_culture.context: It was published in December, just before the author's death. It is a witty classic, famous for the line "Tell me what you eat, and I will tell you what you are."

politics.text: France invades Algiers, beginning a conquest of North Africa that will last for decades.
politics.context: The French landed in June and the city fell in July. The invasion began a conquest of Algeria that lasted until the French left in 1962.

politics.text: Parisians fight for three days in the July Revolution, forcing King Charles X of France to abdicate.
politics.context: The "Three Glorious Days" were in late July. Charles X fled, and Louis-Philippe became king of the French.

society.text: The American Joseph Smith founds a church in upstate New York that grows into the Latter Day Saint movement.
society.context: He founded it in April, a month after publishing the Book of Mormon. It grew into the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

technology.text: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway, the first intercity line run entirely by steam locomotives, opens in England.
technology.context: It opened in September. The politician William Huskisson was killed by a train on opening day.

arts_culture.text: The French painter Eugène Delacroix paints Liberty Leading the People, celebrating the July Revolution in Paris.
arts_culture.context: The woman is Liberty in person, holding the French tricolour flag. The painting was first shown in 1831, and it now hangs in the Louvre.

politics.text: Eighteen-year-old Victoria becomes queen of the United Kingdom on the death of her uncle, King William IV.
politics.context: She became queen in June and reigned for sixty-three years, giving her name to the Victorian era.

society.text: A financial panic spreads from New York as banks stop paying out, and the American economy slides into depression.
society.context: The Panic of 1837 began in May, when New York banks stopped paying out gold and silver. It led to years of unemployment and falling prices.

technology.text: In Britain, William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patent the first commercial electric telegraph.
technology.context: They patented it in June and set up the first line beside a railway. Their system was used on British railways.

arts_culture.text: The Danish author Hans Christian Andersen publishes The Little Mermaid.
arts_culture.context: It appeared in a collection of his fairy tales in the spring. The story is now a classic, and a statue of the mermaid sits in Copenhagen harbour.

politics.text: The Chinese official Lin Zexu destroys thousands of chests of seized British opium at Humen, near Canton.
politics.context: The opium was destroyed in June. Britain sent a fleet the following year.

society.text: The Ottoman sultan's Edict of Gülhane promises equal treatment for all his subjects and begins the Tanzimat reforms.
society.context: It was issued in November in the name of Sultan Abdulmejid I. It promised security of life and property to all subjects, whatever their religion.

technology.text: The French artist Louis Daguerre's photographic process, the daguerreotype, is announced and given free to the world by France.
technology.context: It was announced in January and the details revealed in August. Photographers could make a sharp image on a silvered copper plate, but only one copy.

technology.text: The American inventor Charles Goodyear discovers how to harden rubber by heating it with sulphur, in a process called vulcanisation.
technology.context: He found the process by accident.

arts_culture.text: The English painter J. M. W. Turner exhibits The Fighting Temeraire, showing an old warship being towed to its last berth.
arts_culture.context: It was shown at the Royal Academy in May. The painting shows a veteran warship, at the end of its days, being towed away by a steam tug.

politics.text: Maori chiefs and British officials sign the Treaty of Waitangi at the Bay of Islands.
politics.context: It was signed in February, in what is now New Zealand. It gave Britain sovereignty and promised Maori their lands, but the Maori and English versions differ, causing disputes for generations.

society.text: Britain issues the Penny Black, the world's first adhesive postage stamp, as part of a postal reform led by Rowland Hill.
society.context: It went on sale in May. The sender now paid the postage, at a flat price of one penny for any distance in Britain.

society.text: Queen Victoria marries her cousin Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, in London.
society.context: They married in February. Albert became her closest adviser, and they had nine children.

technology.text: The American inventor Samuel Morse receives a patent for his electric telegraph.
technology.context: The patent was granted in June. His famous first public message followed four years later.

arts_culture.text: The German composer Robert Schumann writes the song cycle Dichterliebe, in a burst of song-writing after marrying Clara Wieck.
arts_culture.context: He married Clara in September after a bitter court battle with her father. The cycle sets poems by Heinrich Heine and became one of the most celebrated of all song cycles.

politics.text: Britain and China sign the Treaty of Nanking, ending the First Opium War and handing over Hong Kong island.
politics.context: It was signed in August aboard a British warship. China paid a large sum and opened five ports to British trade.

society.text: The Illustrated London News publishes its first issue, as the world's first illustrated weekly newspaper.
society.context: It first appeared in May. Its wood-engraved pictures let readers see news events for the first time, at a low price.

technology.text: The American doctor Crawford Long uses ether to put a patient to sleep for an operation, in Jefferson, Georgia.
technology.context: He operated in March, removing a tumour from a patient. He did not publish his results until years later, so others took the credit.

arts_culture.text: The Russian writer Nikolai Gogol publishes Dead Souls, a satirical novel about a swindler who buys dead serfs.
arts_culture.context: It was published in May. Gogol called it a "poem", and it is a classic satire of Russian provincial life.

politics.text: Revolutions spread across Europe, beginning in Sicily and Paris, and toppling King Louis-Philippe of France.
politics.context: The unrest began in January and February. Most of the revolts were put down, but they ended serfdom in the Habsburg lands and brought new constitutions.

society.text: Delegates meet at Seneca Falls, in New York, for the first women's rights convention in the United States.
society.context: It was held in July. The delegates, led by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott, issued a declaration demanding votes for women.

technology.text: The British physicist William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, proposes an absolute temperature scale with a lowest possible temperature.
technology.context: He proposed it in a paper that year. The kelvin, the scientific unit of temperature, is named after him.

arts_culture.text: A group of young English painters founds the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in London, led by Dante Gabriel Rossetti and John Everett Millais.
arts_culture.context: It was founded in September. The group admired Italian painting before Raphael and aimed to paint nature in bright, precise detail.

politics.text: Hong Xiuquan proclaims the Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace in China's Guangxi province, launching the Taiping Rebellion.
politics.context: The revolt began in January and became one of the deadliest wars in history.

society.text: Queen Victoria opens the Great Exhibition in a huge glass hall, the Crystal Palace, in London's Hyde Park.
society.context: It opened in May. About six million people visited the Crystal Palace to see exhibits from around the world.

technology.text: The American inventor Isaac Singer patents a sewing machine that makes sewing at home practical.
technology.context: He patented it in August. It was cheaper and faster than rival machines, and Singer's company sold it widely, including on instalments.

arts_culture.text: The American writer Herman Melville publishes Moby-Dick, a novel about a whaling captain's obsession.
arts_culture.context: It came out in the autumn and sold poorly. Melville died forgotten, and the novel was recognised as a masterpiece only decades later.

politics.text: American Commodore Matthew Perry sails his black ships into Edo Bay, demanding that Japan open to trade.
politics.context: He arrived in July with four warships. The next year Japan signed a treaty opening ports to American ships, ending over two centuries of isolation.

society.text: Baron Haussmann is appointed to rebuild Paris, and begins carving wide boulevards through the old city.
society.context: He was appointed in June by Napoleon III. His rebuilding gave Paris its broad boulevards and uniform buildings, and pushed many poor residents out.

technology.text: The English engineer Sir George Cayley's glider carries a man across a valley in Yorkshire, perhaps the first manned glider flight.
technology.context: The passenger was reportedly his coachman.

arts_culture.text: Giuseppe Verdi's opera La traviata, based on a play by Alexandre Dumas the younger, premieres in Venice.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in March and was a failure at first, partly because of the casting. It was soon revived and became one of the best-loved operas.

politics.text: Indian soldiers in the East India Company's army mutiny at Meerut, and the revolt spreads across northern India.
politics.context: It began in May and spread through northern India. After its defeat, Britain abolished the Company and took over direct rule in 1858.

society.text: The US Supreme Court rules in Dred Scott v. Sandford that a man born into slavery cannot be an American citizen.
society.context: The decision came in March. It said that Black Americans could not be citizens, and it deepened the divide that led to the Civil War.

technology.text: Elisha Otis installs the first safe passenger lift in the Haughwout department store in New York.
technology.context: It went in during March. The safety brake, which stops the lift if the cable breaks, helped make tall buildings practical.

technology.text: The French chemist Louis Pasteur shows that fermentation is caused by living yeast, a step towards germ theory.
technology.context: He published the finding in Lille.

arts_culture.text: The French poet Charles Baudelaire publishes Les Fleurs du mal, and is then prosecuted for offending public morals.
arts_culture.context: It came out in June. Six poems were banned.

arts_culture.text: The French novelist Gustave Flaubert publishes Madame Bovary, a story of provincial adultery, after being tried for obscenity.
arts_culture.context: He was acquitted in February, and the novel came out as a book in April. The trial made it a scandal and a bestseller.

politics.text: The abolitionist John Brown leads a raid on the federal armoury at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, hoping to start a slave uprising.
politics.context: The raid took place in October. Brown was hanged soon after.

politics.text: France and Piedmont-Sardinia defeat Austria at the Battle of Solferino, in the Second Italian War of Independence.
politics.context: It was fought in June. Its horrors inspired Henry Dunant to found the Red Cross.

society.text: A huge solar storm, later named for the British astronomer Richard Carrington, sets telegraph offices alight across the world.
society.context: It hit in early September and lit up the night sky as far south as the Caribbean.

technology.text: The English naturalist Charles Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species, arguing that species evolve by natural selection.
technology.context: It came out in November and sold out on its first day. It argued that living things change slowly over time through natural selection.

technology.text: Work begins on the Suez Canal, under the French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps.
technology.context: Digging began in April. The canal took ten years to build.

arts_culture.text: The English novelist Charles Dickens finishes the weekly serial of A Tale of Two Cities, set in London and Paris.
arts_culture.context: It ran from April to November in Dickens's own magazine, All the Year Round. It opens with the famous words "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times."

arts_culture.text: Giuseppe Verdi's opera A Masked Ball premieres in Rome, after censors force changes to the plot.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in February. Censors forced Verdi to move the story from Sweden to Boston, because it showed the assassination of a king.

politics.text: President Abraham Lincoln issues the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring enslaved people in the rebel states to be free.
politics.context: It took effect on New Year's Day. It did not free all enslaved people at once, but it made ending slavery a goal of the Union in the Civil War.

society.text: Football clubs meet in a London tavern and form the Football Association, laying down the first common rules of the game.
society.context: They met in October at the Freemasons' Tavern. The new rules separated football from rugby and led to the modern game.

technology.text: The world's first underground railway, the Metropolitan Railway, opens in London.
technology.context: It opened in January between Paddington and Farringdon. About thirty thousand passengers rode it on its first day.

arts_culture.text: The French painter Édouard Manet shows Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe at the Salon des Refusés, in Paris, and causes a scandal.
arts_culture.context: It was shown in May at the Salon des Refusés, an exhibition of paintings rejected by the official Salon. Critics were shocked by a nude woman picnicking with clothed men.

politics.text: Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay sign the Treaty of the Triple Alliance against Paraguay.
politics.context: It was signed in May during the Paraguayan War. The war devastated Paraguay and killed a large share of its people.

politics.text: Confederate General Robert E. Lee surrenders to Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House, Virginia.
politics.context: The surrender in April ended the main fighting of the Civil War. Lincoln was assassinated five days later.

society.text: The American states ratify the Thirteenth Amendment, abolishing slavery across the United States.
society.context: It was ratified in December, after the end of the Civil War. It banned slavery and forced labour, except as a punishment for crime.

technology.text: The Austrian monk Gregor Mendel presents his experiments on pea plants to a natural history society in Brno.
technology.context: He read his papers in February and March. His work was ignored until after the turn of the century.

arts_culture.text: The English author Lewis Carroll publishes Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, with drawings by John Tenniel.
arts_culture.context: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Dodgson, an Oxford maths lecturer. He first told the story on a boat trip, to a girl called Alice Liddell.

politics.text: Britain's North American colonies unite as the Dominion of Canada.
politics.context: Confederation took place on the first of July. Canada began as four provinces and later spread across the continent.

society.text: The German thinker Karl Marx publishes the first volume of Das Kapital, his study of capitalism.
society.context: It was published in September. It argued that capitalism exploits workers, and became a basic text of socialism and communism.

technology.text: The Swedish chemist Alfred Nobel patents dynamite, a safe and stable explosive.
technology.context: He patented it in Britain and Sweden.

arts_culture.text: The Austrian composer Johann Strauss the Younger's waltz The Blue Danube premieres in Vienna.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in February. It began as a choral work, and was soon rearranged as an orchestral piece that became Vienna's unofficial anthem.

politics.text: Pro-shogun forces surrender at Hakodate, on the northern Japanese island of Hokkaido, ending the Boshin War.
politics.context: The war ended in May. It cleared the way for the Meiji government.

society.text: A golden spike is driven at Promontory Summit, Utah, joining the Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads across America.
society.context: It was done in May, completing the first transcontinental railroad. A journey that took months by wagon now took about a week.

technology.text: The Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranges the known elements by atomic weight and publishes his periodic table.
technology.context: He published it in March and left gaps for elements not yet found. Later discoveries of gallium and germanium matched his predictions.

technology.text: The Suez Canal opens, linking the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and cutting the sea route from Europe to Asia.
technology.context: It opened in November, with a grand ceremony attended by Empress Eugénie of France.

arts_culture.text: The Russian count Leo Tolstoy completes War and Peace, his vast novel about families and Napoleon's invasion of Russia.
arts_culture.context: The novel was serialised from 1865.

politics.text: King Wilhelm of Prussia is proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.
politics.context: It happened in January, as France was losing the Franco-Prussian War. Germany was united under the Prussian king for the first time.

politics.text: Radical Parisians proclaim the Paris Commune after the French defeat by Prussia.
politics.context: The Commune was proclaimed in March and crushed that May, in a week of savage fighting. Many thousands of Communards were killed.

society.text: A fire that starts in a barn spreads through Chicago and burns for days, destroying much of the city.
society.context: The Great Chicago Fire began in October and burned for about two days. It killed about three hundred people and left a third of the city homeless.

technology.text: Charles Darwin publishes The Descent of Man, applying his theory of natural selection to human origins.
technology.context: It came out in February. Darwin argued that humans share ancestors with apes, which was highly controversial.

arts_culture.text: Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida, set in ancient Egypt, premieres at the Khedivial Opera House in Cairo.
arts_culture.context: It opened on Christmas Eve. The Khedive of Egypt had commissioned it, and it became one of the most popular operas ever written.

politics.text: Benjamin Disraeli becomes British prime minister after the Conservatives win a general election.
politics.context: He took office in February after the Conservatives won a majority. He later made Queen Victoria Empress of India and bought shares in the Suez Canal.

society.text: The explorer Henry Morton Stanley sets out from Zanzibar on an expedition across central Africa.
society.context: He left in November. The journey took nearly three years.

technology.text: The American farmer Joseph Glidden patents barbed wire, which changes the way the Great Plains are farmed.
technology.context: He patented it in November. Cheap, strong wire let farmers fence huge areas, which helped end the open range of the cattle drives.

arts_culture.text: A group of French artists, including Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, hold the first Impressionist exhibition in Paris.
arts_culture.context: It opened in April. A critic mocked a Monet painting called Impression, Sunrise, and the word "Impressionist" stuck.

politics.text: The Ottoman Empire adopts its first written constitution and opens a parliament in Constantinople.
politics.context: The constitution was proclaimed in December. The sultan suspended it within two years.

society.text: Lakota and Cheyenne warriors wipe out Lieutenant Colonel George Custer's US cavalry column at the Little Bighorn, in Montana.
society.context: The battle was fought in June. It was the greatest victory of the Plains Indians over the US Army, but the army soon crushed their resistance.

technology.text: The Scottish-born inventor Alexander Graham Bell is granted a patent for the telephone in the United States.
technology.context: The patent was granted in March. Days later, Bell made the first call, saying "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you."

technology.text: The German engineer Nikolaus Otto builds the first practical four-stroke internal combustion engine.
technology.context: His design became the basis of most petrol engines.

arts_culture.text: Richard Wagner's four-opera Ring cycle is staged complete for the first time at his new opera house in Bayreuth, Germany.
arts_culture.context: It opened the first Bayreuth Festival in August, in a theatre Wagner designed himself. The cycle takes about fifteen hours across four evenings.

politics.text: Queen Victoria is proclaimed Empress of India at a grand durbar in Delhi.
politics.context: The proclamation was on New Year's Day. It marked Britain's direct rule in India, which began after the rebellion of 1857.

society.text: A railway workers' strike spreads across the United States, with riots in Pittsburgh and other cities.
society.context: It began in July when railway companies cut wages. President Hayes sent in federal troops, and about a hundred people died.

technology.text: The American inventor Thomas Edison builds the first phonograph, a machine that records and plays back sound.
technology.context: He demonstrated it in December, reciting "Mary Had a Little Lamb" onto tinfoil.

arts_culture.text: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's ballet Swan Lake premieres at the Bolshoi Theatre, in Moscow.
arts_culture.context: It opened in March, to a poor reception. The staging and dancing were weak, but later productions made it one of the most loved ballets.

politics.text: A Zulu army wipes out a British column at Isandlwana, in southern Africa.
politics.context: It was fought in January, at the start of the Anglo-Zulu War. It was one of the worst defeats the British army suffered at the hands of a native force.

society.text: A railway bridge across the Firth of Tay, in Scotland, collapses in a storm as a train crosses it, killing everyone on board.
society.context: The Tay Bridge disaster happened late in December. About seventy-five people died, and the faulty design led to a public inquiry.

technology.text: The American inventor Thomas Edison perfects a long-lasting electric light bulb at Menlo Park, New Jersey.
technology.context: His first long-lasting lamp worked in October, with a carbonised filament. Edison went on to build a whole electric lighting system.

arts_culture.text: The Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House premieres in Copenhagen and shocks audiences with its ending.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in December. Its heroine leaves her husband at the end, which shocked audiences, and Ibsen had to write an alternative ending for German theatres.

politics.text: Revolutionaries assassinate Tsar Alexander II of Russia with a bomb in Saint Petersburg.
politics.context: He was killed in March, a day after approving reforms. His son Alexander III reversed the reforms and cracked down hard.

society.text: Lawmen and outlaws fight a famous gunfight at the O.K. Corral, in Tombstone, Arizona.
society.context: It happened in October and lasted about thirty seconds. Three men died, and the fight turned Wyatt Earp and his brothers into legends.

technology.text: The German firm Siemens opens the world's first electric tram line, in Lichterfelde, near Berlin.
technology.context: It opened in May. The tram, run by Werner von Siemens's firm, was electric and carried about twenty passengers.

arts_culture.text: The French painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir paints Luncheon of the Boating Party, a lively scene of friends on a balcony above the Seine.
arts_culture.context: He finished it after working on it for a year.

politics.text: France forces the Treaty of Huế on the Vietnamese emperor, making central and northern Vietnam French protectorates.
politics.context: It was signed in August. France ruled Vietnam as a colony for the next seventy years, and China had to accept its control.

society.text: The volcanic island of Krakatoa, between Java and Sumatra, explodes in one of the loudest sounds in recorded history.
society.context: It erupted in August. Its tsunamis killed tens of thousands.

technology.text: The Brooklyn Bridge, with its stone towers and steel cables, opens between New York City and Brooklyn.
technology.context: It opened in May and was the longest suspension bridge in the world at the time. Washington Roebling directed its construction, much of it from a sickbed.

arts_culture.text: The German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche publishes the first part of Thus Spoke Zarathustra, a prose poem about a prophet.
arts_culture.context: He wrote it in a matter of days while living in Italy.

arts_culture.text: The Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson publishes Treasure Island as a book, a pirate adventure narrated by the boy Jim Hawkins.
arts_culture.context: It came out in November. Stevenson wrote it for his stepson, and it set the popular picture of pirates with parrots and treasure maps.

politics.text: The forces of the Mahdi capture Khartoum, in Sudan, and kill the British General Charles Gordon.
politics.context: The city fell in January after a siege of ten months. The Mahdist state ruled Sudan until 1898, when British forces won it back.

politics.text: European powers end the Berlin Conference, agreeing rules for carving up African territory among themselves.
politics.context: The conference closed in February. Not one African ruler had been invited.

society.text: The Statue of Liberty arrives in New York Harbor from France, packed in more than two hundred crates.
society.context: It arrived in June. Its pedestal was not finished until the following year.

technology.text: The German engineer Karl Benz builds a three-wheeled motor car with a petrol engine, a forerunner of the modern car.
technology.context: He built it this year and patented it in January of the next. It had a single-cylinder engine and a top speed of about sixteen kilometres an hour.

arts_culture.text: Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera The Mikado, set in Japan, opens in London.
arts_culture.context: It opened in March and became their most popular work. It ran for nearly seven hundred performances at the Savoy Theatre.

politics.text: The Apache leader Geronimo surrenders to the United States Army in Arizona, ending the last major Indian war.
politics.context: He surrendered in September. The capture ended the Apache Wars, and Geronimo spent the rest of his life as a prisoner of war.

society.text: The Statue of Liberty is dedicated by President Grover Cleveland in New York Harbor.
society.context: The dedication was in October, in front of a huge crowd. France had given the statue to mark the friendship of the two countries.

technology.text: The German engineer Karl Benz receives a patent for his motor car, the first for a practical petrol-driven vehicle.
technology.context: The patent was granted in January. Benz's wife, Bertha, made the first long-distance car trip in one of his cars two years later.

arts_culture.text: The French painter Georges Seurat exhibits A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, made of thousands of tiny dots of colour.
arts_culture.context: It was shown at the last Impressionist exhibition.

politics.text: Brazil's Princess Isabel signs the Golden Law, abolishing slavery.
politics.context: She signed it in May. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery.

politics.text: Wilhelm II becomes German emperor in the Year of the Three Emperors, after the deaths of his grandfather and father.
politics.context: He took the throne in June, after the deaths of Wilhelm I and Frederick III. Wilhelm II later dismissed Bismarck and led Germany into the First World War.

society.text: A huge blizzard paralyses New York and the American north-east, burying cities in snow for days.
society.context: It struck in March. About four hundred people died, and the storm convinced New York to bury its telegraph and telephone wires.

technology.text: George Eastman launches the Kodak camera, a simple box camera that anyone can use.
technology.context: The trademark was registered in the autumn. The slogan was "You press the button, we do the rest".

technology.text: The Serbian-American inventor Nikola Tesla patents his alternating-current motor and power system.
technology.context: The patents were granted in May and later used by George Westinghouse. Alternating current became the main way to send electricity over long distances.

arts_culture.text: The Dutch painter Vincent van Gogh moves to Arles, in the south of France, where he paints his sunflowers and his yellow house.
arts_culture.context: He arrived in February, hoping to set up a community of artists. He painted about two hundred works in Arles, including the sunflowers.

politics.text: Emperor Meiji grants Japan its first modern constitution, creating an elected parliament.
politics.context: The constitution was proclaimed in February. It made Japan the first Asian country with a modern parliament, though the emperor kept great power.

society.text: A dam above Johnstown, Pennsylvania, collapses after heavy rain, and the flood kills more than two thousand people.
society.context: It happened in May. A neglected dam failed after heavy rain and killed more than two thousand people.

technology.text: The engineer Gustave Eiffel's tower is finished in Paris for the World's Fair, making it the tallest structure in the world.
technology.context: It was completed in March and was meant to stand for only twenty years. Many Parisians hated it at first, but it became the symbol of France.

arts_culture.text: The Dutch painter Vincent van Gogh paints The Starry Night while staying in an asylum at Saint-Rémy, in southern France.
arts_culture.context: He painted it in June, from his window, while staying in the asylum. It shows a swirling night sky above a village, and hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

politics.text: France and Russia agree a friendship that grows into an alliance, bringing together two rivals of Germany.
politics.context: The first agreement was in August. It answered Germany's alliances, and it grew into a full military alliance by 1894.

society.text: The Canadian-American teacher James Naismith invents basketball in Springfield, Massachusetts.
society.context: He invented it in December, using peach baskets as hoops. Naismith wanted a game that students could play indoors in winter.

technology.text: Russia begins building the Trans-Siberian Railway, to link Moscow with the Pacific port of Vladivostok.
technology.context: Construction began in May. The railway took about twenty-five years to build and became the longest in the world.

arts_culture.text: The Irish writer Oscar Wilde publishes The Picture of Dorian Gray as a book, a novel about a man whose portrait ages in his place.
arts_culture.context: It came out in the spring as a book, after a shorter magazine version. Critics condemned it as immoral, and it was used against Wilde at his trial in 1895.

politics.text: Japan and China go to war over control of Korea, in the First Sino-Japanese War.
politics.context: War was declared in August. Japan won quickly, and China lost its influence over Korea and had to give up Taiwan.

society.text: Pierre de Coubertin founds the International Olympic Committee at a congress in Paris.
society.context: It was founded in June. The committee organised the first modern Games two years later, in Athens.

technology.text: Tower Bridge opens across the River Thames in London, with a middle section that lifts to let ships through.
technology.context: It opened in June. High walkways let pedestrians cross even when the road section was lifted.

arts_culture.text: Claude Debussy's Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun premieres in Paris.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in December. Its flowing, dreamy sound is often seen as the start of modern music, and it later inspired a famous ballet.

politics.text: Japan and China sign the Treaty of Shimonoseki, ending their war, and China gives Taiwan to Japan.
politics.context: It was signed in April. Japan also won a large payment from China, but Russia, France and Germany forced Japan to give up part of its gains.

society.text: The Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel signs his will, leaving his fortune to fund prizes in his name.
society.context: He signed it in November. The prizes began to be awarded in 1901, and most of his fortune came from dynamite.

technology.text: The German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen discovers X-rays in his laboratory in Würzburg.
technology.context: He found them in November. Röntgen X-rayed his wife's hand, and won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

arts_culture.text: The French brothers Auguste and Louis Lumière show a film to a paying audience, in a Paris café.
arts_culture.context: It was shown on the twenty-eighth of December at the Grand Café. The audience paid one franc to see ten short films, and many call this the birth of cinema.

politics.text: Ethiopian forces under Emperor Menelik II crush an Italian army at Adwa, securing Ethiopia's independence.
politics.context: The battle was fought on the first of March. Ethiopia's victory was one of the few by an African state against a European colonial army, and it stayed independent.

society.text: The first modern Olympic Games open in Athens, the Greek city where the ancient ones began.
society.context: They opened in April, with athletes from fourteen countries. The first winner was the American James Connolly, in the triple jump.

technology.text: The French physicist Henri Becquerel finds that uranium salts fog photographic plates in the dark, revealing radioactivity.
technology.context: He made the discovery in the early part of the year, by accident, after leaving uranium salts and photographic plates in a drawer. Marie Curie later called the effect radioactivity.

technology.text: The Italian inventor Guglielmo Marconi applies in Britain for the first patent on a wireless telegraph system.
technology.context: Marconi was 22. Italy had shown no interest, so he moved to Britain to develop the idea. The patent was granted in 1897.

arts_culture.text: Giacomo Puccini's opera La Bohème, about young artists in Paris, opens in Turin, conducted by Arturo Toscanini.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in February, with Toscanini conducting in Turin. Critics were cool at first, but audiences loved it.

arts_culture.text: Anton Chekhov's play The Seagull premieres in St Petersburg, to a hostile audience.
arts_culture.context: The first night in October was a disaster. A later production by Stanislavski made it a triumph.

politics.text: Theodor Herzl opens the first Zionist Congress in Basel, Switzerland.
politics.context: It opened in August. The congress set up the Zionist movement, which aimed to create a Jewish homeland.

society.text: Gold is found in the Klondike region of Canada, setting off a rush of prospectors to the Yukon.
society.context: The news reached the cities in July. Tens of thousands of people set out for the Klondike, but few found fortunes.

technology.text: The British physicist J. J. Thomson announces the discovery of the electron, the first subatomic particle.
technology.context: He announced it in April. He showed that cathode rays were streams of tiny charged particles, much lighter than atoms.

arts_culture.text: The Irish writer Bram Stoker publishes the vampire novel Dracula.
arts_culture.context: It came out in May. Stoker took the name from a Romanian prince, and the novel set the pattern for vampire stories.

politics.text: Reformers around the Chinese emperor Guangxu launch the Hundred Days' Reform, until Empress Dowager Cixi crushes it.
politics.context: It ran from June to September. The reforms aimed to modernise China, but Empress Dowager Cixi had the emperor imprisoned and several reformers executed.

politics.text: The United States declares war on Spain over Cuba, beginning the Spanish-American War.
politics.context: The declaration was in April. America won within months and took the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam from Spain.

society.text: The American battleship USS Maine explodes in Havana harbour, killing hundreds of sailors and pushing America towards war with Spain.
society.context: It exploded in February. The cause was long disputed.

technology.text: In Paris, Marie and Pierre Curie announce the discovery of two new radioactive elements, polonium and radium.
technology.context: Polonium was announced in July and radium in December. Marie Curie won two Nobel Prizes for her work on radioactivity.

arts_culture.text: The French novelist Émile Zola publishes an open letter in a Paris newspaper accusing the army of a miscarriage of justice.
arts_culture.context: It is known as J'accuse and appeared in January, in L'Aurore, over the Dreyfus affair.

politics.text: Chinese Boxer fighters and imperial troops besiege the foreign legations in Beijing, as an eight-nation force marches to relieve them.
politics.context: The siege lasted from June to August. An eight-nation force relieved the legations, and China was forced to pay a huge indemnity.

society.text: A hurricane destroys the Texas port city of Galveston, in the deadliest natural disaster in American history.
society.context: It struck in September and killed at least six thousand people. The city was later raised and protected with a seawall.

society.text: Paris hosts a World's Fair that welcomes some fifty million visitors, with a moving pavement to carry them past its giant pavilions.
society.context: The Olympic Games were held alongside it, and women competed for the first time. The fair left Paris the Grand Palais and the Petit Palais, and made Art Nouveau fashionable.

technology.text: Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin flies his first rigid airship over Lake Constance, in Germany.
technology.context: It flew in July for about eighteen minutes. Zeppelin airships later carried passengers across the Atlantic, until the Hindenburg disaster.

technology.text: The German physicist Max Planck proposes that energy comes in tiny packets, laying the foundations of quantum theory.
technology.context: He presented the idea in Berlin in December. Planck's "quanta" began the quantum revolution in physics.

arts_culture.text: Giacomo Puccini's opera Tosca premieres in Rome.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in January at the Teatro Costanzi. Critics were cool at first, but audiences loved it, and it remains one of the most performed operas.

politics.text: The six Australian colonies join to form the Commonwealth of Australia.
politics.context: Federation took place on New Year's Day. The new country was a dominion of the British Empire, with its first capital at Melbourne.

society.text: The first Nobel Prizes are awarded in Stockholm.
society.context: They were presented in December, on the anniversary of Nobel's death. The first prizes included physics for Röntgen and peace for Henri Dunant.

technology.text: The Italian inventor Guglielmo Marconi receives the first wireless signal sent across the Atlantic Ocean, in Newfoundland.
technology.context: He received the signal in December, the letter "S" in Morse code sent from Cornwall. Some scientists doubted that he had really heard it.

arts_culture.text: The German writer Thomas Mann publishes his first novel, Buddenbrooks, about the decline of a merchant family.
arts_culture.context: It was published in October. It sold slowly at first, and Mann won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929, largely for this book.

politics.text: The Treaty of Vereeniging ends the Boer War, as the Boer republics accept British rule.
politics.context: The fighting had lasted almost three years. The two Boer republics became British colonies, and were later joined to form the Union of South Africa.

politics.text: Edward the Seventh is crowned in Westminster Abbey, after the ceremony is put off when he needs an emergency operation.
politics.context: The king had appendicitis, and the coronation was delayed from June to August.

society.text: Mount Pelée erupts on the island of Martinique and wipes out the town of Saint-Pierre, killing almost everyone in it.
society.context: Nearly thirty thousand people died. Only a handful survived, among them a prisoner in a thick-walled cell. It was one of the worst volcanic disasters of the century.

technology.text: The American engineer Willis Carrier designs the first modern air conditioning system, to control humidity in a printing works in Brooklyn.
technology.context: The printers' paper swelled and shrank with the weather and spoiled their colour prints. Carrier's method cooled and dried the air. He later founded the Carrier Corporation.

arts_culture.text: Georges Méliès's film A Trip to the Moon shows a rocket landing in the eye of the Man in the Moon.
arts_culture.context: Méliès was a French stage magician. The film was one of the first science fiction films, and used tricks such as double exposures.

politics.text: Panama breaks away from Colombia with American backing, and the United States gains the right to build a canal.
politics.context: Panama declared independence in November, and the United States recognised it within days. The canal was later built across the new country.

politics.text: Russian socialists meet in London and Brussels, and split into Bolsheviks and Mensheviks.
politics.context: The party congress was in the summer. Lenin's faction took the name Bolsheviks, from the Russian word for "majority".

society.text: The first Tour de France sets off from a café near Paris, with sixty cyclists.
society.context: It began in July. The race was created to sell newspapers.

technology.text: The American brothers Orville and Wilbur Wright make the first powered, controlled flights, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.
technology.context: They flew in December. The longest flight that day lasted under a minute.

arts_culture.text: The American writer Jack London publishes The Call of the Wild, a novel about a dog in the Yukon gold rush.
arts_culture.context: It came out in the summer and was an instant success. London drew on his own time in the Klondike gold rush.

politics.text: Japan attacks the Russian fleet at Port Arthur, starting a war that will shock Europe.
politics.context: The attack came without a declaration of war. Japan went on to beat Russia on land and at sea.

politics.text: Britain and France sign the Entente Cordiale, ending old colonial rivalries and settling their disputes over Egypt and Morocco.
politics.context: The agreement was the start of the friendship that bound the two countries together before the First World War.

society.text: A huge fire sweeps through the centre of Baltimore and destroys more than fifteen hundred buildings.
society.context: Fire crews from other cities could not help at first, because their hose couplings did not fit Baltimore's hydrants.

society.text: Seven European football associations found FIFA, the body that will organise the World Cup.
society.context: The first World Cup took place in Uruguay in 1930.

society.text: St. Louis hosts a huge World's Fair, the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, which draws visitors from across the United States and the world.
society.context: It is remembered for its racist ethnographic displays, which showed Filipino, Native American, African and other people as living exhibits. The Olympic Games were held there too.

technology.text: The New York City subway opens, with trains running underground from City Hall to Harlem.
technology.context: Thousands rode it on the first evening. Private companies built and ran the early lines, and the city took over later.

technology.text: John Ambrose Fleming, a British engineer, patents the vacuum tube diode, the first electronic valve and a step towards radio.
technology.context: The valve could turn alternating current into direct current. It was also called the thermionic valve, or the Fleming valve.

arts_culture.text: Puccini's opera Madama Butterfly, about a Japanese girl abandoned by an American naval officer, premieres at La Scala in Milan.
arts_culture.context: The first night was a disaster and the audience jeered. Puccini revised it, and a new version was a success in Brescia a few months later.

arts_culture.text: Anton Chekhov's last play, The Cherry Orchard, opens at the Moscow Art Theatre, and Chekhov dies a few months later.
arts_culture.context: The play is a comedy about a noble family that loses its estate. Chekhov died in July of tuberculosis.

politics.text: Japan's navy destroys the Russian fleet at the Battle of Tsushima, a stunning defeat for a European power.
politics.context: It happened in May, during the Russo-Japanese War. Japan's win astonished the world and ended the war to Russia's humiliation.

politics.text: Troops fire on a peaceful march of workers in Saint Petersburg on Bloody Sunday, sparking a revolution across Russia.
politics.context: It happened in January. The shootings turned many workers against the tsar and led to strikes and mutinies throughout the year.

society.text: The British viceroy Lord Curzon divides the Indian province of Bengal, sparking a nationalist campaign of boycotts.
society.context: The partition took effect in October. It split the province along religious lines, and was reversed in 1911 after fierce protests.

technology.text: Albert Einstein, a young physicist working in a Swiss patent office, publishes papers on relativity and the photoelectric effect.
technology.context: It is known as his "miracle year". He published four landmark papers.

arts_culture.text: A group of French painters led by Henri Matisse, soon nicknamed the "wild beasts", shocks visitors at the Salon d'Automne in Paris.
arts_culture.context: The show was in October. The critic Louis Vauxcelles gave them the name Fauves.

politics.text: Persia's first parliament, the Majlis, opens in Tehran after the Constitutional Revolution forces the shah to agree.
politics.context: It opened in October. The shah was forced to accept a constitution, which made Persia one of the first Middle Eastern states with a parliament.

society.text: A huge earthquake and fire destroy much of San Francisco.
society.context: It struck in April and fires burned for days. About three thousand people died, and most of the city's people lost their homes.

technology.text: Britain launches HMS Dreadnought, a battleship so powerful that it makes every older warship look outdated.
technology.context: She was launched at Portsmouth in February and finished in about a year. Her speed and heavy guns started a naval arms race with Germany.

arts_culture.text: The French painter Paul Cézanne, often called the father of modern art, dies in Aix-en-Provence.
arts_culture.context: He died in October, after being caught in a storm while painting. Cézanne's work inspired Picasso and the Cubists.

politics.text: Britain and Russia sign an entente in St Petersburg, settling their rivalries in Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet.
politics.context: It joined Britain, France and Russia in the Triple Entente, which faced Germany and Austria-Hungary in the First World War.

politics.text: In Finland, nineteen women are elected to parliament, in the first election in Europe open to women candidates.
politics.context: Finland was then a grand duchy under the Russian empire. It had given women the vote the year before.

society.text: Robert Baden-Powell takes twenty boys to Brownsea Island in England for a camp that starts the Scout movement.
society.context: The boys came from different backgrounds. Baden-Powell, a hero of the Boer War, published Scouting for Boys the following year.

technology.text: The liner Lusitania sails from Liverpool on her first voyage, one of the fastest ships in the world.
technology.context: She soon won the Blue Riband for the fastest crossing of the Atlantic. She was sunk by a German submarine in 1915.

arts_culture.text: Pablo Picasso finishes Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, a shocking painting of five women whose faces look like African masks.
arts_culture.context: The painting broke the rules of perspective. It is often seen as the start of Cubism. Picasso kept it hidden in his studio for years.

politics.text: Young Turk army officers force the Ottoman sultan Abdul Hamid II to restore the constitution.
politics.context: The revolution began in July. The sultan agreed to restore the parliament, though he was deposed the following year.

society.text: A huge explosion flattens about two thousand square kilometres of forest in Siberia, near the Tunguska River.
society.context: It happened in June. The cause was probably a meteor exploding in the air.

technology.text: The Ford Motor Company in Detroit introduces the Model T, a cheap and sturdy car designed for ordinary families.
technology.context: It went on sale in October. Henry Ford's assembly line later cut its price, and about fifteen million were eventually sold.

arts_culture.text: The Scottish writer Kenneth Grahame publishes The Wind in the Willows, a tale of a Mole, a Rat and a Toad.
arts_culture.context: It came out in October. It began as bedtime stories that Grahame told his young son, and it remains a classic of children's literature.

arts_culture.text: The Austrian painter Gustav Klimt completes The Kiss, a couple wrapped in gold leaf, in Vienna.
arts_culture.context: It was shown in Vienna in the summer, and bought by the Austrian state. It is Klimt's best-known work.

politics.text: Japan's elder statesman Itō Hirobumi is shot dead by a Korean nationalist at a railway station in Manchuria.
politics.context: Itō had been Japan's first prime minister. His killer, An Jung-geun, is honoured as a hero in Korea. Japan annexed Korea the next year.

society.text: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People is founded in New York by W. E. B. Du Bois, Ida B. Wells and others.
society.context: It was founded on the hundredth anniversary of Abraham Lincoln's birth. Other founders included Mary White Ovington, William English Walling and Oswald Garrison Villard.

technology.text: The Belgian-born chemist Leo Baekeland announces Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, to the American Chemical Society.
technology.context: Bakelite was hard, cheap and did not conduct electricity, so it was used for radios, telephones and many other goods. He had developed it in 1907.

arts_culture.text: The Russian composer Sergei Rachmaninoff plays the first performance of his Third Piano Concerto, in New York.
arts_culture.context: It is famous as one of the hardest piano concertos. Rachmaninoff wrote it for his first American tour.

arts_culture.text: In Paris, the impresario Sergei Diaghilev opens a season of Russian ballet and opera that amazes audiences.
arts_culture.context: The company was not yet called the Ballets Russes, a name it took the following year. Its star dancers included Vaslav Nijinsky.

politics.text: Francisco Madero calls for a revolt against Mexican president Porfirio Díaz, beginning the Mexican Revolution.
politics.context: The call to arms came in November. The revolution lasted about ten years and ended the long rule of Díaz.

politics.text: Portugal's monarchy is overthrown in a revolution, and a republic is declared in Lisbon.
politics.context: The revolution was in October. King Manuel II fled to Britain, and Portugal became a republic.

society.text: Halley's Comet blazes in the night sky and the Earth passes through its tail, causing panic in some places.
society.context: The Earth passed through the tail in May. Some people bought gas masks and "comet pills" for protection, though no harm came.

technology.text: The French engineer Georges Claude shows the first neon lamp to the public, in Paris.
technology.context: He showed it in December. Neon lighting soon filled shop signs around the world.

arts_culture.text: Igor Stravinsky's ballet The Firebird premieres in Paris, danced by the Ballets Russes.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in June. The music made Stravinsky famous and led to his even more shocking The Rite of Spring three years later.

politics.text: An army uprising at Wuchang, in China, begins the revolution that will overthrow the Qing dynasty.
politics.context: It began in October. By the next February the last emperor had abdicated and China was a republic.

society.text: The Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen and his team reach the South Pole.
society.context: They arrived in December. Robert Falcon Scott's party reached the Pole a month later and found they had been beaten.

technology.text: The New Zealand-born physicist Ernest Rutherford proposes that atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus at their centre.
technology.context: He announced his model in Manchester.

arts_culture.text: The Mona Lisa is stolen from the Louvre, in Paris, by an Italian workman, Vincenzo Peruggia.
arts_culture.context: It was stolen in August and recovered two years later in Florence. The theft made the painting world-famous.

politics.text: Puyi, the last child emperor of China's Qing dynasty, abdicates after the Xinhai Revolution.
politics.context: He gave up the throne in February. China became a republic.

politics.text: African leaders meet in Bloemfontein and found the organisation that becomes the African National Congress.
politics.context: It was founded in January, as the South African Native National Congress. It was renamed the African National Congress in 1923.

society.text: The British explorer Robert Falcon Scott reaches the South Pole and finds a Norwegian flag already planted there.
society.context: He reached the Pole in January. None of his party survived the return.

technology.text: The Austrian physicist Victor Hess rides a balloon to great height and discovers cosmic rays.
technology.context: The flight was in August. He found that radiation increases with altitude.

arts_culture.text: The Spanish painter Pablo Picasso glues a piece of oilcloth onto a canvas in Paris, creating his first collage.
arts_culture.context: The work is Still Life with Chair Caning, an early landmark of Cubism. Its oval shape imitates a café table, and the "frame" is a piece of rope.

politics.text: American forces occupy the Mexican port of Veracruz, during the Mexican Revolution.
politics.context: They landed in April. President Wilson ordered the occupation after American sailors were arrested, and it lasted about seven months.

politics.text: At Tannenberg, a German army under Hindenburg and Ludendorff destroys the Russian Second Army, whose commander shoots himself.
politics.context: The battle ended the Russian invasion of East Prussia and made Hindenburg a national hero.

society.text: British and German soldiers stop fighting and meet in no man's land on Christmas Day.
society.context: The truce was spontaneous and unofficial.

technology.text: The Panama Canal opens, letting ships sail between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
technology.context: The first ship passed through in August. The canal saved ships the long voyage around South America.

technology.text: A German U-boat sinks the British cruiser HMS Pathfinder, the first warship sunk by a submarine's self-propelled torpedo.
technology.context: It happened in September off the coast of Scotland. The sinking showed how dangerous submarines could be.

arts_culture.text: Charlie Chaplin first appears as the Tramp, in a short film made in Venice, California.
arts_culture.context: The film was released in February. The Tramp, with his bowler hat and cane, became one of the most famous characters in cinema.

politics.text: Italy abandons its old allies and joins Britain and France in the war, after a secret treaty promises it Austrian lands.
politics.context: Italy had been allied with Germany and Austria-Hungary before the war. It declared war on Austria-Hungary in May. Many of the promised lands were never handed over.

society.text: A German submarine torpedoes the liner Lusitania off Ireland, and more than a thousand people die, many of them Americans.
society.context: The ship carried shells and ammunition as well as passengers. The sinking turned many Americans against Germany, though the United States stayed out of the war until 1917.

technology.text: At Ypres in Belgium, German troops release chlorine gas from cylinders on a large scale for the first time, choking Allied soldiers.
technology.context: It was the first big gas attack on the Western Front. Gas masks soon followed. Both sides used poison gas for the rest of the war.

technology.text: In Berlin, Albert Einstein presents the final equations of his general theory of relativity, a new theory of gravity.
technology.context: He lectured on it to the Prussian Academy of Sciences in November. The theory explained a small oddity in the orbit of Mercury.

arts_culture.text: In Prague, Franz Kafka's story The Metamorphosis, about a man who wakes up as a giant insect, is published.
arts_culture.context: It first appeared in a German magazine in October. Kafka worked as an insurance clerk, and most of his work came out after his death.

politics.text: Irish rebels led by Patrick Pearse seize the General Post Office in Dublin and declare an Irish republic, in the Easter Rising.
politics.context: The rising lasted less than a week and was crushed by British troops. The execution of its leaders afterwards turned many Irish people towards the rebels.

politics.text: On the first day of a huge British offensive on the Somme, the army suffers its worst losses, with tens of thousands killed or wounded.
politics.context: There were about sixty thousand British casualties and about twenty thousand dead. The battle went on for months.

society.text: Margaret Sanger opens the first birth control clinic in the United States, in the Brownsville district of Brooklyn.
society.context: Police closed the clinic within days and arrested her. Her campaign helped lead to the legal spread of birth control.

society.text: The central span of the Quebec Bridge, a giant steel bridge over the St Lawrence River in Canada, falls into the water during construction.
society.context: Workers were lifting the centre span into place when it fell. The bridge had collapsed once before, while it was being built. It opened the next year.

technology.text: British tanks are used in battle for the first time, lumbering across northern France at Flers-Courcelette.
technology.context: The first tanks were slow and often broke down, but they frightened German troops. The French were upset because they had wanted to wait and use many tanks at once.

arts_culture.text: In neutral Zürich, artists at the Cabaret Voltaire launch Dada, an anti-war art movement that mocks logic and tradition.
arts_culture.context: Poets and artists such as Hugo Ball and Tristan Tzara performed nonsense poems and noise music. Dada began as a protest against the war.

politics.text: The British government issues the Balfour Declaration, supporting a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine.
politics.context: It was issued in November. The letter promised British support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine, and it shaped the region's later history.

politics.text: Under President Woodrow Wilson, the United States declares war on Germany, bringing fresh troops and money to the Allies.
politics.context: Wilson cited German attacks on neutral ships by submarine. The Zimmermann Telegram had turned American opinion.

society.text: A ship loaded with explosives blows up in Halifax harbour, in Canada, in the largest man-made explosion of its time.
society.context: It happened in December. It killed about two thousand people and flattened part of the city.

technology.text: British tanks attack in large numbers for the first time at the Battle of Cambrai, in France.
technology.context: The battle began in November. The tanks broke through German lines, though most of the gains were soon lost.

technology.text: British naval codebreakers decode the Zimmermann Telegram, in which Germany proposes an alliance with Mexico against the United States.
technology.context: The codebreakers worked in the Admiralty's Room 40. The telegram was sent in January. Britain passed it to the Americans, and it was made public in March.

arts_culture.text: The French artist Marcel Duchamp submits a porcelain urinal signed "R. Mutt", titled Fountain, to an exhibition in New York.
arts_culture.context: It was submitted in April, and the committee refused to show it. It is now seen as a landmark of modern art.

politics.text: President Woodrow Wilson sets out his Fourteen Points, a plan for a fair peace and a new league of nations, in a speech to Congress.
politics.context: The speech was made in January. The points called for open diplomacy, free seas and self-rule for many peoples. Germany later asked for an armistice on that basis.

politics.text: Russia's new Bolshevik government signs the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany, ending its part in the war and giving up huge lands.
politics.context: Lenin accepted harsh terms to end the fighting. Germany could then move many troops to the Western Front.

society.text: Parliament passes a law giving the vote to women over thirty and to all men over twenty-one, a huge change for Britain's voters.
society.context: Women had to be over thirty, and meet property rules. Women won the vote on equal terms with men in 1928.

society.text: A new and deadly strain of flu starts to spread around the world, and will later be called the Spanish flu.
society.context: It killed tens of millions of people. It was called Spanish because Spain's newspapers, free from wartime censorship, reported it openly.

technology.text: Germany's Paris Gun, a giant long-range cannon, begins shelling Paris from more than a hundred kilometres away.
technology.context: Its shells climbed so high that they reached the stratosphere. It was the longest-range gun ever used, but it did little military damage.

technology.text: Britain creates the Royal Air Force, the world's first independent air force, by merging its army and navy flying services.
technology.context: It was formed on 1 April, by joining the Royal Flying Corps and the Royal Naval Air Service. By the end of the war it was the largest air force in the world.

arts_culture.text: The English war poet Wilfred Owen is killed in action while leading his men across the Sambre-Oise Canal in France.
arts_culture.context: Owen died on 4 November, one week before the Armistice ended the war. Only a few of his poems appeared in his lifetime, but Dulce et Decorum Est and others made him the best-known poet of the war.

politics.text: British troops open fire on an unarmed crowd at the Jallianwala Bagh, in Amritsar, India.
politics.context: The massacre took place in April. Troops killed hundreds, and the shock turned many Indians against British rule.

politics.text: The Allies and Germany sign the Treaty of Versailles in the Hall of Mirrors, formally ending the First World War with Germany.
politics.context: It was signed in June. The treaty made Germany accept blame for the war and pay large reparations.

politics.text: In Paris, a young Vietnamese nationalist, later known as Ho Chi Minh, petitions the Allied leaders at Versailles for his country's rights.
politics.context: He used the name Nguyen Ai Quoc, meaning Nguyen the Patriot. The leaders, including Woodrow Wilson, ignored him, and he later turned to communism.

society.text: A giant tank of molasses bursts in Boston, Massachusetts, sending a sticky wave through the streets.
society.context: It burst in January. The wave killed twenty-one people and ran through the streets at about thirty-five miles an hour.

technology.text: Astronomers led by Arthur Eddington photograph a solar eclipse from the island of Príncipe, off West Africa, to test Einstein's theory.
technology.context: The May observations supported Einstein's predictions. Newspapers announced that his theory had overthrown Newton's, and he became a celebrity.

arts_culture.text: The German architect Walter Gropius founds the Bauhaus school of art and design in Weimar.
arts_culture.context: It opened in April. The school's blend of art, craft and technology shaped modern design and architecture.

politics.text: The League of Nations holds its first council meeting, in Paris.
politics.context: It met in January. The League was meant to prevent war, but the United States never joined.

politics.text: Polish forces under Józef Piłsudski beat the Red Army at the gates of Warsaw, in a victory called the Miracle on the Vistula.
politics.context: The Soviets had hoped to carry communism west into Germany. The battle was fought in August, and Poland kept its independence.

society.text: Prohibition begins in the United States, banning the making and selling of alcoholic drinks.
society.context: It took effect in January. It led to bootlegging and organised crime, and was repealed in 1933.

technology.text: Station KDKA in Pittsburgh makes the first scheduled commercial radio broadcast, reporting the results of a presidential election.
technology.context: It broadcast in November, with the news of Warren Harding's victory. Radio then spread quickly across America.

arts_culture.text: The German film The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari premieres in Berlin and sets the style of expressionist cinema.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in February. Its twisted sets and painted shadows made it a landmark of German expressionist cinema.

politics.text: Adolf Hitler takes over as leader of the Nazi Party in Munich, after a power struggle with its founders.
politics.context: He had joined the small party two years earlier. His speeches drew crowds, and he demanded absolute control.

politics.text: A truce ends the Irish War of Independence, after more than two years of fighting between the IRA and British forces.
politics.context: The truce began in July. A treaty followed in December, creating the Irish Free State, but it also split Irish republicans into two sides.

society.text: A white mob attacks the Black neighbourhood of Greenwood in Tulsa, Oklahoma, killing many people and burning homes and businesses.
society.context: Greenwood was known as Black Wall Street. The official toll was thirty-six, but historians believe up to three hundred died. The massacre was long left out of history books.

society.text: Two Italian immigrants and anarchists, Sacco and Vanzetti, are found guilty of murder in Massachusetts, in a trial many thought unfair.
society.context: They were executed in 1927, after years of protests around the world.

technology.text: Frederick Banting and Charles Best in Toronto extract insulin, the hormone that will save millions of people with diabetes.
technology.context: They worked in a laboratory lent by John Macleod. The first patient was treated in January 1922. Banting and Macleod shared the Nobel Prize in 1923.

technology.text: Coco Chanel launches a perfume in Paris, made with synthetic ingredients, that will become one of the most famous in the world.
technology.context: The perfume is called Chanel No. 5. It was first given to a few select clients in May.

arts_culture.text: Charlie Chaplin's film The Kid, about the Tramp and an abandoned child, premieres and makes Jackie Coogan a child star.
arts_culture.context: It was Chaplin's first full-length film. It mixed comedy with sadness. The premiere was in January.

arts_culture.text: Jaroslav Hašek begins publishing The Good Soldier Švejk, a comic Czech novel about a simple soldier who bumbles through the First World War.
arts_culture.context: The book came out in parts from 1921 until Hašek's death in 1923, and was never finished. It is one of the most translated Czech novels.

politics.text: Benito Mussolini's Blackshirts march on Rome, and the king of Italy invites him to form a government.
politics.context: The march took place in October. Mussolini became the youngest prime minister in Italian history and soon ruled as a dictator.

politics.text: The Ottoman sultanate is abolished, ending the rule of a dynasty that lasted more than six centuries.
politics.context: The sultanate was abolished in November. The last sultan, Mehmed VI, left the country on a British warship.

society.text: The English archaeologist Howard Carter finds the tomb of the pharaoh Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings, in Egypt.
society.context: He found the first steps in November and entered the burial chamber later. It was the best-preserved royal tomb ever found in Egypt, and made headlines around the world.

technology.text: Canadian doctors in Toronto give insulin to a boy dying of diabetes, the first patient treated with it.
technology.context: The patient was Leonard Thompson, aged fourteen, in January. Frederick Banting led the work.

arts_culture.text: The Irish writer James Joyce's novel Ulysses is published in Paris, on his fortieth birthday.
arts_culture.context: It was published in February by Sylvia Beach, at her Paris bookshop. It was banned in the United States and Britain for years as obscene.

politics.text: Mustafa Kemal, later called Atatürk, proclaims the Republic of Turkey.
politics.context: He proclaimed it in October. Atatürk became its first president and ruled until his death in 1938.

politics.text: Adolf Hitler and his Nazis attempt to seize power in a failed coup in a Munich beer hall.
politics.context: The Beer Hall Putsch was in November. It failed, and Hitler was jailed, where he wrote Mein Kampf.

society.text: A huge earthquake strikes Tokyo and Yokohama, in Japan, and fires destroy much of both cities.
society.context: The Great Kantō earthquake struck on the first of September. The quake and the fires that followed killed more than one hundred thousand people.

technology.text: The Russian-born engineer Vladimir Zworykin applies for a patent for the iconoscope, an early television camera tube.
technology.context: He applied in December. Zworykin's electronic camera tube helped make electronic television possible.

arts_culture.text: The brothers Walt and Roy Disney found a small cartoon studio in Hollywood, California.
arts_culture.context: It was set up in October. The studio went on to create Mickey Mouse and Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs.

politics.text: Vladimir Lenin, the founder of the Soviet state, dies near Moscow.
politics.context: He died in January. Joseph Stalin won the struggle to succeed him, and Petrograd was renamed Leningrad.

society.text: The first Winter Olympic Games are held in Chamonix, in the French Alps.
society.context: They opened in January. Athletes from sixteen countries took part in the winter sports.

technology.text: Two American Army aircraft complete the first flight around the world, after nearly six months.
technology.context: They finished in September. The flight took 175 days and covered more than forty thousand kilometres, with many stops.
