arts_culture.text: George Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue premieres at a concert in New York, with the composer at the piano.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in February. The piece mixed jazz and classical music, and its opening clarinet glissando is famous.

politics.text: Benito Mussolini tells parliament that he takes full responsibility for fascist violence, in a speech that starts his dictatorship.
politics.context: He challenged his opponents to charge him, and nobody dared. Italy soon became a one-party state.

politics.text: Winston Churchill, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, announces that Britain is returning to the gold standard.
politics.context: The pound became too expensive for exporters, and coal and other industries suffered. Economists such as Keynes criticised the move.

society.text: A teacher, John Scopes, is put on trial in Dayton, Tennessee, for teaching evolution, in a case nicknamed the Monkey Trial.
society.context: The lawyers Clarence Darrow and William Jennings Bryan faced each other. Scopes was fined one hundred dollars, and the verdict was later overturned on a technicality.

society.text: Teams of sled dogs race through a blizzard to bring medicine to Nome, Alaska, where children are dying of diphtheria.
society.context: The dog Balto led the last stretch. The race inspired the Iditarod and a famous statue in New York's Central Park.

technology.text: In London, John Logie Baird transmits the first television pictures with shades of grey, of a ventriloquist's dummy.
technology.context: He had earlier sent only black-and-white outlines. A dummy called Stooky Bill was the subject. Public demonstrations followed the next year.

arts_culture.text: F. Scott Fitzgerald publishes The Great Gatsby, a novel of wealth, parties and lost love on Long Island.
arts_culture.context: It sold poorly at first, and Fitzgerald died believing it a failure. It later became one of the most famous American novels.

politics.text: Hirohito becomes emperor of Japan, beginning the Shōwa era.
politics.context: He took the throne on Christmas Day. His reign, until 1989, was the longest of any Japanese emperor.

society.text: A general strike by British trade unions in support of coal miners brings the United Kingdom to a halt.
society.context: The General Strike lasted nine days in May. It began over miners' pay and failed when the unions called it off.

technology.text: The American physicist Robert Goddard launches the world's first liquid-fuelled rocket in Massachusetts.
technology.context: It was launched in March, and flew for only about two and a half seconds. Goddard's rockets paved the way for space flight.

technology.text: The Scottish inventor John Logie Baird demonstrates a working television system in London.
technology.context: He gave the demonstration in January to members of the Royal Institution. His pictures were very blurry, but the machine worked.

arts_culture.text: The English author A. A. Milne publishes Winnie-the-Pooh, with drawings by E. H. Shepard.
arts_culture.context: It came out in October. The stories were inspired by Milne's son Christopher Robin and his toy bear.

politics.text: Chiang Kai-shek's forces turn on their Communist allies in Shanghai, in a bloody purge.
politics.context: It happened in April. Chiang's purge of the Communists began a civil war that lasted over twenty years.

society.text: The American pilot Charles Lindbergh flies solo and non-stop from New York to Paris.
society.context: He landed in May after flying for about thirty-three hours. Lindbergh became a worldwide hero.

technology.text: The young American inventor Philo Farnsworth demonstrates the first fully electronic television system, in San Francisco.
technology.context: The first image was transmitted in September. It was a simple straight line.

arts_culture.text: Fritz Lang's science-fiction film Metropolis premieres in Berlin.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in January. It was one of the most expensive silent films ever made, and its robot became a cinema icon.

politics.text: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist forces take the old imperial capital, Beijing, and nominally reunify China.
politics.context: The Northern Expedition captured the city in June. China was then united in name, though regional warlords still held power.

society.text: British women win the vote on the same terms as men, when Parliament passes the Equal Franchise Act.
society.context: The voting age for women was lowered to 21.

technology.text: The Scottish bacteriologist Alexander Fleming notices a mould killing bacteria on a forgotten dish in London, and discovers penicillin.
technology.context: The discovery was in September. It led to the first antibiotic, and Fleming shared a Nobel Prize in 1945.

arts_culture.text: Walt Disney's cartoon mouse, Mickey, whistles his way through the short film Steamboat Willie in New York.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in November, with synchronised sound. It is often counted as Mickey Mouse's debut.

arts_culture.text: The German playwright Bertolt Brecht and the composer Kurt Weill's The Threepenny Opera premieres in Berlin.
arts_culture.context: It opened in August and includes the song Mack the Knife. It was a hit in Germany and later in the rest of the world.

politics.text: The Lateran Treaty is signed, creating the Vatican City as an independent state inside Rome.
politics.context: It was signed in February by Mussolini's government and the Pope. It settled a conflict between the Papacy and the Italian state that had lasted since 1870.

society.text: The New York stock market crashes, and a long worldwide depression begins.
society.context: The crash came in late October. It began a worldwide economic depression that lasted through the 1930s.

technology.text: The airship Graf Zeppelin flies around the world, carrying passengers.
technology.context: The flight took place in August, and took about three weeks. It was a world first for a passenger airship.

arts_culture.text: The Belgian cartoonist Hergé creates Tintin, the boy reporter, for a children's newspaper supplement.
arts_culture.context: The first story began in January. Tintin became one of the most popular comic characters in Europe.

politics.text: Mahatma Gandhi leads the Salt March to the sea at Dandi, to protest against the British salt tax.
politics.context: It began in March. Gandhi's march of about 240 miles ended when he picked up salt from the sea.

society.text: Uruguay hosts and wins the first football World Cup, in Montevideo.
society.context: The final was in July. Uruguay beat Argentina four goals to two, in a tournament of only thirteen teams.

technology.text: The American astronomer Clyde Tombaugh discovers Pluto, at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona.
technology.context: The discovery was announced in March. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

arts_culture.text: The American painter Grant Wood paints American Gothic, a stern farmer and his daughter in front of a house.
arts_culture.context: It was exhibited in Chicago in the autumn. Wood's painting of a farmer and his daughter became one of the best-known American images.

politics.text: King Alfonso the Thirteenth of Spain leaves the country, and a republic is proclaimed.
politics.context: Republicans had won the big cities in local elections. The republic lasted until the Spanish Civil War ended in 1939.

politics.text: A bomb damages a railway line near Mukden in Manchuria, and Japan uses it as an excuse to invade the region.
politics.context: Japan blamed Chinese soldiers, but the blast was staged by Japanese officers. Japan then set up a puppet state called Manchukuo.

society.text: The gangster Al Capone is found guilty of tax evasion in Chicago, and later sentenced to eleven years in prison.
society.context: Capone had been too powerful to convict of his violent crimes. He served time in Alcatraz and died in 1947.

technology.text: The Empire State Building opens in New York and becomes the tallest building in the world.
technology.context: It was built in about a year during the Great Depression. It held the height record for almost forty years.

arts_culture.text: Charlie Chaplin's silent film City Lights, in which the Tramp loves a blind flower seller, premieres as talking films take over.
arts_culture.context: Chaplin refused to make a talking picture, and added only music and sound effects. It ends with one of the most famous scenes in cinema.

arts_culture.text: Universal's film Frankenstein, with Boris Karloff as the monster, is released and sets off a craze for horror films.
arts_culture.context: Dracula, starring Bela Lugosi, had come out earlier in the year. Both made huge profits for Universal.

politics.text: Abdulaziz ibn Saud proclaims the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, uniting his territories under one name.
politics.context: The kingdom was proclaimed in September. Oil was discovered in the country six years later.

society.text: The American aviator Amelia Earhart becomes the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean.
society.context: She flew in May, from Newfoundland to Northern Ireland. The flight took under fifteen hours.

society.text: The Sydney Harbour Bridge opens, linking the north and south shores of the Australian city.
society.context: It opened in March. The bridge, nicknamed "the Coathanger", was the largest steel arch bridge in the world.

technology.text: The English physicist James Chadwick discovers the neutron at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge.
technology.context: He announced it in February. The neutron has no electric charge, which made it ideal for splitting atoms. Chadwick won a Nobel Prize for the discovery.

arts_culture.text: The English writer Aldous Huxley publishes Brave New World, a novel about a future society controlled by pleasure.
arts_culture.context: It came out in the winter. The book was banned in some countries for its views on sex and drugs.

politics.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt takes office as president of the United States, telling Americans they have nothing to fear but fear itself.
politics.context: The country was deep in the Great Depression, with banks failing. Within days he closed the banks for a holiday and began the New Deal.

politics.text: A fire destroys the Reichstag, Germany's parliament building, and the Nazis use it as an excuse to take sweeping powers.
politics.context: A young Dutch communist was arrested for the fire. The Nazis blamed the communists and passed an emergency decree the next day.

society.text: The Twenty-first Amendment ends Prohibition in the United States, and Americans can legally buy alcohol again.
society.context: Prohibition had lasted for thirteen years and fuelled organised crime. Cities celebrated with open bars.

technology.text: Two British aircraft fly over Mount Everest for the first time, carrying cameras to photograph the summit.
technology.context: The expedition was led by Lord Clydesdale, an RAF pilot and later a duke. The flight showed the summit could be seen from the air.

arts_culture.text: The film King Kong premieres in New York, with a giant ape climbing the Empire State Building.
arts_culture.context: The ape was a model brought to life by stop-motion animation. Fay Wray starred as the woman he carries. It was a huge hit in the Depression.

politics.text: Adolf Hitler has rivals and enemies murdered in a purge later called the Night of the Long Knives.
politics.context: The victims included Ernst Röhm, leader of the SA stormtroopers. Hitler claimed they planned a revolt. The killings won him the army's support.

politics.text: President Hindenburg dies, and Hitler combines the posts of chancellor and president and takes the title Führer.
politics.context: The army swore an oath of loyalty to Hitler himself. A referendum later approved the change.

society.text: Host nation Italy beats Czechoslovakia in the final of the second football World Cup, in Rome.
society.context: Mussolini used the tournament for propaganda. Italy won in extra time.

society.text: President Franklin Roosevelt signs a law that takes gold out of American money and puts the nation's gold in government hands.
society.context: It was signed in January. In 1933, Americans had been ordered to hand in their gold coins. The law also raised the official price of gold from about twenty dollars to thirty-five an ounce.

technology.text: Irène and Frédéric Joliot-Curie create artificial radioactivity for the first time, in Paris.
technology.context: They made a radioactive form of phosphorus by bombarding aluminium. They won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry the next year. Irène was Marie Curie's daughter.

arts_culture.text: Agatha Christie publishes Murder on the Orient Express, in which Hercule Poirot solves a killing on a snowbound train.
arts_culture.context: It was published in Britain at the start of the year. The story was partly inspired by a real train stuck in snow.

arts_culture.text: Donald Duck makes his first screen appearance, in the Disney cartoon The Wise Little Hen.
arts_culture.context: Donald was a bad-tempered duck who pretended to have a stomach ache to avoid work. He became one of Disney's biggest stars.

politics.text: Italy invades Ethiopia, and Emperor Haile Selassie appeals to the League of Nations for help in vain.
politics.context: Italian forces used poison gas and modern weapons against Ethiopian troops. The League's mild sanctions did not stop Mussolini.

politics.text: Germany's Nuremberg Laws strip Jews of citizenship and ban marriages between Jews and other Germans.
politics.context: The laws were announced at a Nazi Party rally in Nuremberg in September.

society.text: The boxer James Braddock, a former dock worker nicknamed the Cinderella Man, wins the world heavyweight title in a huge upset.
society.context: Braddock had been on relief during the Depression. He beat Max Baer over fifteen rounds in New York. Russell Crowe later played him in a film.

society.text: Persia officially becomes Iran, as Reza Shah asks other countries to use the name its own people have long used.
society.context: The shah announced the change at the Persian new year, in March. Westerners had long called the country Persia, but Iran is an old name for the land.

society.text: Voters in the Saar, run by the League of Nations since the First World War, overwhelmingly choose to rejoin Germany in a referendum.
society.context: About nine in ten voted to return, in January. Hitler had been in power for two years, and the Nazis celebrated the result as a propaganda success.

technology.text: President Roosevelt dedicates the Hoover Dam on the Colorado River, then the largest dam and concrete structure in the world.
technology.context: Thousands of workers built it during the Great Depression, and more than a hundred died. It created Lake Mead.

technology.text: DuPont chemist Wallace Carothers makes nylon, the first fully synthetic fibre.
technology.context: Nylon was used for stockings and parachutes. DuPont launched it to the public five years later.

technology.text: Parker Brothers begins selling the board game Monopoly, which becomes a hit during the Depression.
technology.context: The game came from earlier games about land and rent. Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers.

arts_culture.text: George Gershwin's opera Porgy and Bess opens, with an all-Black cast of classically trained singers and the song Summertime.
arts_culture.context: It had tryouts in Boston before opening in New York. Some critics were unsure at first, but it became a classic.

arts_culture.text: Alfred Hitchcock's spy thriller about an innocent man on the run across Scotland, with a mysterious ring of spies, is released.
arts_culture.context: The film is called The 39 Steps and was based on a novel by John Buchan. It made Hitchcock Britain's top director.

politics.text: Italian forces under Marshal Pietro Badoglio enter Addis Ababa and capture Ethiopia's capital.
politics.context: They entered in May. Emperor Haile Selassie went into exile.

politics.text: General Francisco Franco leads a military uprising against Spain's elected government, beginning the Spanish Civil War.
politics.context: The uprising began in July. The war lasted almost three years and ended with Franco ruling Spain as a dictator.

society.text: The American athlete Jesse Owens wins four gold medals at the Berlin Olympic Games, in front of Adolf Hitler.
society.context: The Games took place in August. Owens's victories challenged the Nazi idea of racial superiority.

technology.text: The British mathematician Alan Turing publishes his paper on computable numbers, describing an imaginary machine that can compute anything.
technology.context: His paper laid the foundation for computer science.

technology.text: The BBC begins the world's first regular public high-definition television service, from Alexandra Palace in London.
technology.context: The service started in November. It was suspended during the Second World War and returned in 1946.

arts_culture.text: Charlie Chaplin's film Modern Times, about a factory worker and the machine age, is released in the United States.
arts_culture.context: It came out in February. Chaplin plays the Tramp, who struggles with the assembly line in a factory.

politics.text: Japanese and Chinese troops clash at the Marco Polo Bridge, near Beijing, starting a full-scale war.
politics.context: It happened in July. The clash grew into the Second Sino-Japanese War, which merged with the Second World War.

society.text: The German airship Hindenburg bursts into flames as it lands in New Jersey.
society.context: It happened in May, as the airship was about to moor. Thirty-six people died, and the disaster ended the age of passenger airships.

technology.text: The British engineer Frank Whittle runs the first jet engine on a test bed in Rugby, England.
technology.context: The test was in April. The engine was not used in a plane until 1941, but it began the jet age.

arts_culture.text: Pablo Picasso paints Guernica, a huge black-and-white protest against the bombing of a Basque town.
arts_culture.context: He painted it in Paris in the spring. It was shown in the Spanish pavilion at the world fair, and became a symbol of the horrors of war.

politics.text: Mexican president Lázaro Cárdenas nationalises the country's oil industry, taking it from foreign companies.
politics.context: He announced it in March. Mexico took over the foreign oil firms, and the date is still celebrated.

society.text: Nazi mobs attack Jewish homes, shops and synagogues across Germany and Austria in the Kristallnacht pogrom.
society.context: It took place on the night of the ninth to the tenth of November. About ninety Jews were killed and tens of thousands were arrested.

technology.text: German chemists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann split the uranium atom in Berlin, discovering nuclear fission.
technology.context: The experiment was in December. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained it.

arts_culture.text: Orson Welles's radio drama of The War of the Worlds convinces some American listeners that Martians are invading.
arts_culture.context: It was broadcast in October, on the eve of Halloween. Reports of mass panic have since been shown to be exaggerated.

arts_culture.text: Superman, created by two young Americans, Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster, first appears on the cover of Action Comics.
arts_culture.context: The comic went on sale in the spring. Superman became the first superhero of the modern comic book.

politics.text: Germany and the Soviet Union sign a pact promising not to fight each other, and secretly agree to divide up Poland and other lands.
politics.context: These two bitter enemies shocked the world. Germany invaded Poland a little over a week later, and the Soviets followed.

politics.text: General Franco's forces take Madrid, and the Spanish Civil War ends in victory for his side.
politics.context: Franco ruled Spain as dictator until his death in 1975.

society.text: The Black singer Marian Anderson gives a free concert at the Lincoln Memorial after being refused the use of a Washington hall.
society.context: She was barred by the Daughters of the American Revolution. Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from the group in protest, and about seventy-five thousand people came to hear her.

technology.text: Albert Einstein signs a letter to President Roosevelt warning that Germany might build an atomic bomb.
technology.context: The letter was written by the physicist Leo Szilard. It helped start the American effort that became the Manhattan Project.

technology.text: Two Stanford friends, Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard, start a company in a garage in Palo Alto, California.
technology.context: Their first product was an audio oscillator, which Walt Disney bought for Fantasia. The garage is called the birthplace of Silicon Valley.

arts_culture.text: Gone with the Wind premieres in Atlanta, a lavish Civil War epic starring Vivien Leigh and Clark Gable.
arts_culture.context: It became one of the most successful films ever and won ten Oscars. Its Black cast members could not attend the Atlanta premiere because of segregation.

arts_culture.text: The Wizard of Oz, with Judy Garland as Dorothy, is released, using new Technicolor to show Oz in vivid colour.
arts_culture.context: It was not a big hit at first. It became a classic through television repeats.

arts_culture.text: Batman makes his first appearance in Detective Comics, created by Bob Kane and Bill Finger.
arts_culture.context: The comic was published in the spring. Batman became one of the most famous superheroes ever.

politics.text: Winston Churchill becomes Britain's prime minister, on the day Germany attacks the Low Countries and France.
politics.context: He took over from Neville Chamberlain, who resigned. Churchill formed a government of all parties.

politics.text: A fleet of warships and small civilian boats rescues about three hundred thousand Allied soldiers from the beaches of Dunkirk.
politics.context: The evacuation lasted more than a week. The army left its heavy equipment behind. Churchill called it a miracle of deliverance.

politics.text: Leon Trotsky, exiled Soviet revolutionary, is attacked with an ice axe in Mexico and dies the next day.
politics.context: The attacker was an agent of Stalin's secret police. Trotsky had been Lenin's partner in the revolution.

society.text: The Chicago Bears beat the Washington Redskins seventy-three to nothing in the NFL championship game, the biggest win in its history.
society.context: The Bears used the T formation. Washington had narrowly beaten them in the regular season.

society.text: German bombers begin the Blitz, attacking London night after night.
society.context: The bombing began in September and went on for months. Londoners sheltered in Underground stations.

society.text: The Nazis open the Auschwitz concentration camp in occupied Poland, which will become the largest site of the Holocaust.
society.context: It began as a prison camp for Polish political prisoners. Later it became the main extermination camp.

technology.text: Howard Florey's team at Oxford shows that penicillin protects mice from deadly infection, proving it can work as a medicine.
technology.context: The test was in May. Florey and Ernst Chain had picked up work that Alexander Fleming began years earlier. They shared a Nobel Prize with him.

technology.text: The Vought-Sikorsky helicopter, designed by Igor Sikorsky, makes its first free flight in the United States.
technology.context: Sikorsky is called the father of the practical helicopter. His designs led to the helicopters we know today.

arts_culture.text: Charlie Chaplin's film The Great Dictator mocks Hitler, with Chaplin playing both a Jewish barber and a dictator.
arts_culture.context: It was Chaplin's first full talking picture. It ends with a long speech calling for peace and humanity.

arts_culture.text: Disney's Fantasia sets animation to classical music, with Mickey Mouse as the sorcerer's apprentice.
arts_culture.context: The film used a new sound system with several speakers. It lost money at first but is now a classic.

politics.text: Rudolf Hess, Hitler's deputy, parachutes into Scotland on a strange flight to try to make peace with Britain.
politics.context: He was arrested and spent the rest of his life in prison. Many people still wonder why he made the flight.

politics.text: President Roosevelt signs the Lend-Lease Act, letting the United States send weapons to Britain and its allies without being paid at once.
politics.context: The United States was not yet at war. Roosevelt called America the arsenal of democracy.

politics.text: In his State of the Union speech, Roosevelt names four freedoms that people everywhere should enjoy.
politics.context: They were freedom of speech, freedom of worship, freedom from want and freedom from fear.

society.text: Joe DiMaggio begins a baseball hitting streak that will run for fifty-six games, a record that has never been beaten.
society.context: The streak ended in July. DiMaggio played for the New York Yankees and was married to Marilyn Monroe later.

society.text: Work on Mount Rushmore ends, with the faces of four presidents carved into a mountainside in South Dakota.
society.context: The presidents are Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Lincoln. The sculptor Gutzon Borglum died that year.

technology.text: The German engineer Konrad Zuse demonstrates the first working programmable, fully automatic computer, in Berlin.
technology.context: It used telephone relays, not electronics. The machine was destroyed in an air raid, and a copy was built later.

technology.text: In Oxford, a policeman dying of infection becomes one of the first patients treated with penicillin.
technology.context: He improved, but the supply ran out and he died. It showed the drug's promise, and the need to make much more of it.

arts_culture.text: Orson Welles's Citizen Kane, about a newspaper tycoon whose last word is Rosebud, premieres in New York.
arts_culture.context: Welles was twenty-five when he made it. It is often named the greatest film ever made, though it did not make money at first.

arts_culture.text: John Huston's film The Maltese Falcon, with Humphrey Bogart as the detective Sam Spade, is released.
arts_culture.context: It was Huston's first film as director. Many call it the first great film noir.

politics.text: Nazi officials meet at a villa at Wannsee near Berlin to organise the deportation and murder of Europe's Jews.
politics.context: Reinhard Heydrich chaired the meeting. The killings had already begun, and the meeting arranged how the whole system would work.

politics.text: About eighty thousand British and Commonwealth troops surrender at Singapore, in Britain's worst defeat of the war.
politics.context: Japanese forces had advanced down the Malay peninsula. Churchill called it the worst disaster in British military history.

politics.text: The British Eighth Army under Bernard Montgomery attacks the Germans at El Alamein in Egypt, in a turning point in North Africa.
politics.context: Churchill said that before Alamein the British never had a victory. The battle ended German hopes of reaching the Suez Canal.

society.text: A fire at the Cocoanut Grove nightclub in Boston kills almost five hundred people, one of the worst nightclub fires ever.
society.context: The exits were blocked or locked. The fire led to new fire safety laws and to advances in treating burns.

society.text: President Roosevelt signs an order that leads to Japanese Americans being forced from their homes into internment camps.
society.context: More than a hundred thousand people were moved, most of them American citizens. The government apologised decades later.

technology.text: Enrico Fermi's team in Chicago starts the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction, under the stands of a university football field.
technology.context: The reactor was called Chicago Pile-One. The experiment was a key step towards the atomic bomb.

technology.text: Stephen Hawking, the future physicist who will explain black holes, is born in Oxford.
technology.context: He was born on the three-hundredth anniversary of Galileo's death. He lived with motor neurone disease for most of his life.

arts_culture.text: Casablanca, with Humphrey Bogart and Ingrid Bergman, has its world premiere in New York, soon after Allied troops land in North Africa.
arts_culture.context: The film was released more widely early the next year. It won the Oscar for Best Picture. The song As Time Goes By became famous.

arts_culture.text: Bing Crosby records White Christmas, which becomes the best-selling single of all time.
arts_culture.context: Irving Berlin wrote the song for the film Holiday Inn. It reminded soldiers far from home of Christmas.

arts_culture.text: At the Oscars, How Green Was My Valley beats Citizen Kane for best picture.
arts_culture.context: Citizen Kane won only for its screenplay. The Oscars were held in February.

politics.text: Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin meet together for the first time, in Tehran, to plan the final defeat of Germany.
politics.context: They agreed that the Western Allies would invade France the next year. It was the first of the Big Three conferences.

politics.text: Italy announces its surrender to the Allies, but German troops quickly seize control of most of the country.
politics.context: Mussolini had been overthrown in July. The Germans rescued him and set up a puppet state in the north.

politics.text: Joseph Goebbels gives his total war speech to a Berlin crowd, asking whether they want a war more total than anything imagined.
politics.context: The speech was made in a Berlin sports hall. It came weeks after the German defeat at Stalingrad.

society.text: A terrible famine in Bengal, in British India, kills millions of people, as wartime policies and shortages cut off food.
society.context: Estimates of the dead range from about two to three million. Historians blame wartime policies and the loss of rice imports from Burma.

society.text: Jewish fighters in the Warsaw Ghetto rise up against the Nazis, in the largest Jewish revolt of the war.
society.context: The Germans burned the ghetto to put the revolt down. The fighters held out for weeks against far better armed troops.

technology.text: British codebreakers test Colossus, the first electronic computer built to break German codes, at Bletchley Park.
technology.context: It was designed by Tommy Flowers. Its existence was kept secret for decades after the war.

technology.text: Lancaster bombers drop Barnes Wallis's bouncing bombs on German dams in the Ruhr, in the Dambusters raid.
technology.context: The bombs skipped over the water and sank next to the dam wall. Two dams were broken, and many of the planes were lost.

technology.text: The Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann takes LSD on purpose for the first time and goes home on his bicycle, on what is now called Bicycle Day.
technology.context: He had felt strange effects a few days earlier, when a little got on his fingers. His bicycle ride became legendary.

arts_culture.text: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's story The Little Prince is published in New York, while the author is in exile from occupied France.
arts_culture.context: Saint-Exupéry was an airman and wrote and drew it himself. He disappeared on a flight the next year. It became one of the most translated books ever.

arts_culture.text: Rodgers and Hammerstein's Oklahoma! opens on Broadway, reshaping the musical.
arts_culture.context: Its songs and dances moved the story forward instead of just entertaining. It ran for more than two thousand performances.

politics.text: Army officers led by Claus von Stauffenberg try to kill Hitler with a bomb in a briefcase, but he survives.
politics.context: The plot was in July. Hitler had thousands of suspects arrested and many executed.

politics.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt wins an unprecedented fourth term as US president, beating Thomas Dewey.
politics.context: No president had won more than two terms before him. He died a few months into the fourth term.

politics.text: Delegates from forty-four countries meet at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire and agree on a new world money system.
politics.context: The agreement created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

society.text: Anne Frank and the others hiding with her in an Amsterdam annexe are betrayed and arrested by the Gestapo.
society.context: They had hidden for over two years. Anne died in Bergen-Belsen in early 1945. Her father Otto survived and published her diary.

society.text: The future baseball star Jackie Robinson, then an army officer, is arrested for refusing to move to the back of a bus at Fort Hood.
society.context: He was court-martialled but cleared. Three years later he became the first Black player in the major leagues.

technology.text: Germany fires the world's first long-range ballistic missiles, the dreaded V rockets, at targets in Paris and London.
technology.context: The rocket was the V-2. It travelled faster than sound, so there was no warning. After the war, the V-2's engineers helped build American and Soviet space rockets.

arts_culture.text: Laurence Olivier's film of Shakespeare's Henry the Fifth, made in colour in wartime, premieres in London to boost morale.
arts_culture.context: Olivier directed and starred in it. It was dedicated to the airborne troops. It opened up Shakespeare to film audiences.

arts_culture.text: At the Oscars, Casablanca wins best picture.
arts_culture.context: The ceremony was held at Grauman's Chinese Theatre in Hollywood. Casablanca had premiered in New York the year before.

arts_culture.text: The famously out-of-tune soprano Florence Foster Jenkins sings at Carnegie Hall to a sold-out house.
arts_culture.context: Her shows were a sensation because she was so bad and did not know it. A film about her was made decades later with Meryl Streep.

politics.text: Labour wins a landslide election, and Clement Attlee replaces Winston Churchill as Britain's prime minister, weeks after victory in Europe.
politics.context: Churchill had led Britain through the war, but voters wanted social reform at home. Attlee's government went on to create the National Health Service.

politics.text: Delegates from fifty countries sign the United Nations Charter in San Francisco.
politics.context: The UN was meant to prevent another world war. Poland signed a little later, which made fifty-one founding members.

society.text: The Nuremberg trials open, putting leading Nazis before an international court for war crimes and crimes against humanity.
society.context: They began in November in a German city where the Nazis had held huge rallies. Several defendants were sentenced to death.

technology.text: In the New Mexico desert, American scientists under J. Robert Oppenheimer set off the first atomic bomb, in the Trinity test.
technology.context: The test took place on a July morning. Within a month, atomic bombs were dropped on Japan.

technology.text: An American bomber drops the first atomic bomb ever used in war on the Japanese city of Hiroshima, and Nagasaki is hit three days later.
technology.context: The attacks killed well over a hundred thousand people. Japan announced its surrender within days.

arts_culture.text: Rodgers and Hammerstein's musical Carousel opens on Broadway, with the song You'll Never Walk Alone.
arts_culture.context: The show is based on a Hungarian play by Ferenc Molnár. It opened in April and ran for more than eight hundred performances.

politics.text: The Philippines becomes independent from the United States, after nearly half a century of American rule.
politics.context: Independence came on the fourth of July. The United States had promised it before the war, and the war delayed it.

society.text: Judges at Nuremberg, in Germany, deliver verdicts on leading Nazis, sentencing twelve to death.
society.context: The verdicts came in October. Twelve were sentenced to death, and the trials set the pattern for later war crimes courts.

technology.text: The first general-purpose electronic computer, ENIAC, is unveiled at the University of Pennsylvania.
technology.context: It was unveiled in February. ENIAC filled a large room and could do thousands of sums a second.

arts_culture.text: The French writer and director Jean Cocteau releases his film Beauty and the Beast, based on the fairy tale.
arts_culture.context: It was released in the autumn. Its dreamlike sets and costumes made it a classic of French cinema.

politics.text: Britain divides India into two independent countries, India and Pakistan, in a partition that displaces millions.
politics.context: The partition took place in August. It led to mass migration and violence, and perhaps a million people died.

society.text: Jackie Robinson plays his first game for the Brooklyn Dodgers, breaking baseball's colour bar.
society.context: It was in April. Robinson became the first Black player in modern major-league baseball.

technology.text: Researchers at Bell Laboratories in New Jersey demonstrate the first working transistor.
technology.context: The demonstration was in December. Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley shared a Nobel Prize for it.

technology.text: The American pilot Chuck Yeager breaks the sound barrier in a rocket plane over California.
technology.context: The flight was in October, in a Bell X-1. Yeager flew faster than the speed of sound for the first time.

arts_culture.text: A young Dutch girl's diary, written while hiding from the Nazis in Amsterdam, is first published.
arts_culture.context: Anne Frank's Het Achterhuis appeared in June, edited by her father Otto. It has since been translated into more than seventy languages.

arts_culture.text: The first Edinburgh International Festival is held in Scotland, bringing theatre and music to a war-weary Britain.
arts_culture.context: It opened in August. The festival has grown into one of the biggest arts festivals in the world.

politics.text: David Ben-Gurion proclaims the State of Israel in Tel Aviv, and neighbouring Arab states invade.
politics.context: It was proclaimed in May. Neighbouring Arab states invaded the next day, starting the first Arab-Israeli war.

society.text: The Indian leader Mahatma Gandhi is shot dead in New Delhi by a Hindu nationalist, Nathuram Godse.
society.context: He was killed on the last day of January, on his way to evening prayers. Gandhi had been working for peace between Hindus and Muslims.

technology.text: Columbia Records in New York introduces the long-playing vinyl record, which holds about twenty minutes per side.
technology.context: It was introduced in June. The new disc held much more music than the old shellac discs, and set the standard for albums.

arts_culture.text: The Italian director Vittorio De Sica releases Bicycle Thieves, a neorealist film about a poor Roman whose bicycle is stolen.
arts_culture.context: It was released in November. It was filmed on location with non-professional actors, and won an honorary Oscar.

politics.text: Mao Zedong proclaims the People's Republic of China from the Gate of Heavenly Peace in Beijing.
politics.context: He proclaimed it on the first of October. The Communists had won the civil war, and the Nationalists fled to Taiwan.

politics.text: Twelve countries sign the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington, creating the NATO alliance.
politics.context: It was signed in April. The members agreed that an attack on one would be an attack on all.

society.text: South Africa passes a law banning marriages between white and non-white people, early in its apartheid programme.
society.context: The Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act passed in the summer. More apartheid laws followed in the next years.

technology.text: The Soviet Union tests its first atomic bomb at a site in Kazakhstan.
technology.context: The test was in August, sooner than Western experts had expected. It ended the American monopoly on atomic weapons.

arts_culture.text: The English writer George Orwell publishes his novel of a totalitarian future, in which Big Brother watches everyone.
arts_culture.context: It came out in June. The book gave us phrases such as "Big Brother" and "doublethink".

politics.text: North Korean forces cross the border into South Korea, beginning the Korean War.
politics.context: The invasion began in late June. The three-year war ended in a stalemate, with the border near where it began.

politics.text: India becomes a republic and adopts its constitution, with Rajendra Prasad as its first president.
politics.context: It came into force on the twenty-sixth of January. India became the world's largest democracy.

society.text: Diners Club issues the first general-purpose charge card in New York, starting the credit card age.
society.context: It was issued in February. Frank McNamara reportedly got the idea after forgetting his wallet at a restaurant.

technology.text: The British mathematician Alan Turing publishes a paper asking whether machines can think, and proposes an imitation game.
technology.context: It appeared in the journal Mind in October. The game is now called the Turing test.

arts_culture.text: The American cartoonist Charles Schulz launches the comic strip Peanuts, featuring Charlie Brown and Snoopy.
arts_culture.context: It first appeared in October. The strip ran for fifty years, and Schulz drew every one himself.

politics.text: Army officers overthrow King Farouk of Egypt in a coup led by the Free Officers.
politics.context: The coup was in July. Colonel Gamal Abdel Nasser soon became the country's leader.

politics.text: King George the Sixth dies in his sleep at Sandringham, and his young daughter Elizabeth becomes queen.
politics.context: Elizabeth was in Kenya when her father died. She was crowned the following year.

society.text: A thick smog settles over London and kills thousands of people, in the Great Smog.
society.context: It lasted for several days in December. Thousands of people died, and the smog led to Britain's Clean Air Act.

technology.text: The United States tests the first hydrogen bomb, at Enewetak Atoll in the Pacific Ocean.
technology.context: The test was in November. The explosion destroyed the small island of Elugelab.

technology.text: Britain tests its first atomic bomb on the Montebello Islands off Western Australia, becoming the third nuclear power.
technology.context: The bomb was exploded inside a ship, in a test called Operation Hurricane, in October.

arts_culture.text: The American writer Ernest Hemingway publishes The Old Man and the Sea.
arts_culture.context: It came out in September. The novella won the Pulitzer Prize and helped Hemingway win the Nobel Prize.

politics.text: Iran's prime minister, Mohammad Mosaddegh, is overthrown in a coup backed by American and British intelligence agencies.
politics.context: He was removed in August. The Shah returned to power.

politics.text: The Soviet leader Joseph Stalin dies at his dacha near Moscow, after almost three decades in power.
politics.context: He died in March. His death led to a power struggle, and Nikita Khrushchev eventually took over.

society.text: The New Zealand beekeeper Edmund Hillary and the Sherpa climber Tenzing Norgay reach the summit of Mount Everest.
society.context: They reached the top in May, as part of a British expedition. The news reached London on the morning of the Queen's coronation.

society.text: The young Queen Elizabeth II is crowned in Westminster Abbey, in a ceremony broadcast on television to millions.
society.context: The coronation was in June. It was the first coronation to be broadcast on television.

technology.text: James Watson and Francis Crick, two researchers at Cambridge, describe the double-helix structure of DNA.
technology.context: The paper was published in April. It built on X-ray pictures taken by Rosalind Franklin.

arts_culture.text: Samuel Beckett's play Waiting for Godot, in which two men wait for someone who never arrives, premieres in a small Paris theatre.
arts_culture.context: It opened in January. Critics were baffled at first, and it is now seen as a landmark of twentieth-century theatre.

politics.text: Vietnamese forces under General Võ Nguyên Giáp defeat the French at Dien Bien Phu.
politics.context: The battle ended in May. The defeat led France to leave Indochina, and Vietnam was divided.

society.text: The British runner Roger Bannister runs the first mile in under four minutes, at Oxford.
society.context: He did it in May. The run took three minutes and fifty-nine seconds.

technology.text: The United States launches Nautilus, the world's first nuclear-powered submarine.
technology.context: It was launched in January. The submarine could stay underwater for months.

arts_culture.text: The Japanese film Godzilla, about a giant monster awakened by nuclear tests, premieres in Tokyo.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in November. The monster was a symbol of the fear of nuclear weapons, and it led to dozens of sequels.

politics.text: Leaders of twenty-nine Asian and African countries meet at Bandung, in Indonesia, to oppose colonialism.
politics.context: The conference was in April. It brought together countries that did not want to take a side in the Cold War.

society.text: Rosa Parks refuses to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, and is arrested, sparking a bus boycott.
society.context: It happened on the first of December. The bus boycott lasted over a year and made Martin Luther King Jr. a national leader.

society.text: Disneyland opens in Anaheim, California.
society.context: It opened in July. It was one of the first modern theme parks.

technology.text: The American researcher Jonas Salk's polio vaccine is declared safe and effective.
technology.context: The announcement came in April. Mass vaccination brought polio cases down dramatically.

technology.text: The physicist Albert Einstein, who developed the theory of relativity, dies in Princeton, New Jersey.
technology.context: A few days earlier he had signed a warning against nuclear weapons, together with Bertrand Russell. The warning was published after his death.

arts_culture.text: The Indian director Satyajit Ray releases his first film, Pather Panchali, about a poor family in rural Bengal.
arts_culture.context: It was released in August. The film won international prizes and brought Indian cinema to a world audience.

arts_culture.text: The Museum of Modern Art in New York opens The Family of Man, a huge exhibition of photographs about human life, curated by Edward Steichen.
arts_culture.context: It showed more than five hundred photographs from dozens of countries. It then toured the world for years, and millions of people saw it.

politics.text: Israel, Britain and France attack Egypt after President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalises the Suez Canal.
politics.context: The attack came in October. Under heavy pressure, the three countries withdrew.

politics.text: Soviet tanks crush the Hungarian uprising in Budapest.
politics.context: The revolution began in October and was put down in early November. Thousands were killed, and many Hungarians fled abroad.

society.text: Melbourne becomes the first city in the southern hemisphere to host the Summer Olympic Games.
society.context: They opened in November. Because of Australia's strict quarantine rules, the equestrian events were held in Stockholm.

technology.text: IBM, in California, introduces the first commercial computer with a hard disk drive, the RAMAC.
technology.context: It was announced in September. The machine's disks could store about five million characters.

arts_culture.text: The young American singer Elvis Presley releases his first album and is soon a national sensation.
arts_culture.context: The album came out in March, after the single Heartbreak Hotel. It was the first rock and roll album to top the American charts.

politics.text: Ghana becomes the first sub-Saharan African colony to win independence from Britain, under Kwame Nkrumah.
politics.context: Independence came in March. It inspired other African colonies to demand their own independence.

politics.text: Six European countries sign the Treaty of Rome, founding the European Economic Community.
politics.context: It was signed in March, in the Italian capital. The treaty began the European Economic Community, the forerunner of the European Union.

society.text: Nine Black students, escorted by federal troops, enter Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas.
society.context: They entered in September, on the order of President Eisenhower. The crisis was one of the first big tests of the Supreme Court's ruling against school segregation.

technology.text: The Soviet Union launches Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, from Baikonur in Kazakhstan.
technology.context: It was launched in October and started the space race. Its beeping signal could be heard by radio listeners around the world.

arts_culture.text: Jack Kerouac publishes On the Road, a novel about restless friends driving across America, which he typed on one long scroll.
arts_culture.context: It came out in September. It became a bible of the Beat Generation.

arts_culture.text: Leonard Bernstein's musical West Side Story, a modern retelling of Romeo and Juliet, opens on Broadway.
arts_culture.context: It opened in September. The show's music and dancing changed American musical theatre.

politics.text: Mao Zedong launches the Great Leap Forward, an attempt to industrialise China very fast.
politics.context: It began in the early part of the year. The campaign to industrialise by force ended in a great famine that killed millions.

society.text: The Brussels World's Fair opens with the Atomium, a giant model of an iron crystal.
society.context: It opened in April. The Atomium, built from nine steel spheres, became the symbol of Brussels.

technology.text: The American engineer Jack Kilby demonstrates the first working integrated circuit at Texas Instruments.
technology.context: He demonstrated it in September. Integrated circuits led to the microchip and modern computers, and Kilby won a Nobel Prize in 2000.

technology.text: The United States creates NASA, a civilian space agency, in answer to the Soviet lead in space.
technology.context: Congress passed the law and President Eisenhower signed it in July. NASA began work in October and took over from an older research body.

arts_culture.text: The Nigerian writer Chinua Achebe publishes Things Fall Apart.
arts_culture.context: It was published in June. It is one of the most widely read African novels, and shows how colonial rule disrupted a Nigerian village.

politics.text: Fidel Castro's rebels take Havana as the dictator Fulgencio Batista flees Cuba.
politics.context: Batista left at the very start of the year.

society.text: The Dalai Lama flees Tibet for India after a failed uprising against Chinese rule in Lhasa.
society.context: He escaped in March and set up a government in exile in India.

technology.text: A Soviet space probe crashes into the Moon on purpose, the first human-made object to reach another world.
technology.context: The probe was Luna 2, in September. It carried Soviet emblems, and its instruments showed that the Moon has no strong magnetic field.

arts_culture.text: The American trumpeter Miles Davis records Kind of Blue, one of the best-selling jazz albums of all time.
arts_culture.context: It was released in August. It is often called the best-selling jazz album of all time.

politics.text: The Belgian Congo becomes independent, with Patrice Lumumba as its first prime minister.
politics.context: Independence was declared on the last day of June. Lumumba was dismissed within months and killed in 1961, and the country fell into a long crisis.

politics.text: John F. Kennedy narrowly wins the American presidential election, defeating Richard Nixon.
politics.context: The vote was in November. At forty-three, Kennedy became the youngest man ever elected president.

society.text: The most powerful earthquake ever recorded strikes southern Chile, near the city of Valdivia.
society.context: It struck in May. The quake reached magnitude 9.5, and its tsunami crossed the Pacific as far as Japan.

technology.text: The American physicist Theodore Maiman operates the first working laser, in California.
technology.context: He did it in May. The laser is now used in everything from eye surgery to barcode scanners.

arts_culture.text: Alfred Hitchcock's thriller Psycho, with its famous shower scene, is released.
arts_culture.context: It opened in June. The shower murder shocked audiences, and the film helped invent the modern thriller and slasher genres.

arts_culture.text: Harper Lee publishes To Kill a Mockingbird, a novel about racial injustice in a small Alabama town, seen through the eyes of a young girl.
arts_culture.context: It came out in July and won the Pulitzer Prize the next year. Lee based the lawyer Atticus Finch partly on her own father, who was also a lawyer.

politics.text: Cuban exiles trained by the CIA land at the Bay of Pigs and are crushed by Fidel Castro's forces.
politics.context: The invasion took place in April. It was a humiliating failure for President Kennedy and pushed Castro closer to the Soviet Union.

politics.text: East German authorities begin building the Berlin Wall, dividing the city.
politics.context: The barrier went up overnight in August. It stopped East Germans from fleeing to the West, and stood for twenty-eight years.

society.text: The trial of Adolf Eichmann, a chief organiser of the Holocaust, opens in Jerusalem.
society.context: It opened in April. Eichmann was found guilty and hanged in 1962, in Israel's only civilian execution.

society.text: Black and white activists ride buses through the American South to challenge segregation, as the Freedom Riders.
society.context: The first rides left Washington in May. The riders were attacked by mobs, and their courage helped force an end to segregation in bus stations.

technology.text: The Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin becomes the first person in space, orbiting the Earth once in Vostok.
technology.context: The flight took place in April and lasted under two hours. Gagarin returned a world hero.

arts_culture.text: Audrey Hepburn stars as Holly Golightly in the film Breakfast at Tiffany's, based on a novella by Truman Capote.
arts_culture.context: It was released in October. Hepburn's black dress became one of the most famous costumes in film.

politics.text: Algeria becomes independent from France after a bitter war of independence.
politics.context: Independence came on the third of July. The war had lasted nearly eight years, and hundreds of thousands of French settlers left.

society.text: The American biologist Rachel Carson publishes Silent Spring, a warning about pesticides that inspires the environmental movement.
society.context: It came out in September. The book warned of the damage caused by the pesticide DDT, which was later banned in the United States.

technology.text: The communications satellite Telstar is launched, and sends the first live television pictures across the Atlantic.
technology.context: It was launched in July. It relayed the first live television pictures between America and Europe.

arts_culture.text: The first James Bond film, Dr. No, premieres in London, starring Sean Connery.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in October. The film began one of the longest-running film series in history.

arts_culture.text: The Rolling Stones, a new band led by Mick Jagger and Keith Richards, play their first concert at the Marquee Club in London.
arts_culture.context: They played blues songs. The band had formed only weeks earlier, and went on to become one of the longest-running rock bands.

politics.text: French president Charles de Gaulle vetoes Britain's first attempt to join the European Economic Community.
politics.context: He said Britain was not ready to be a true European partner. He vetoed a second application in 1967. Britain finally joined in 1973.

politics.text: John Profumo, Britain's war minister, resigns after admitting he lied to Parliament about his affair with Christine Keeler.
politics.context: The Profumo affair mixed sex, spying and politics, and badly damaged the Conservative government of Harold Macmillan.

society.text: A bomb planted by white racists explodes at a Black church in Birmingham, Alabama, and kills four young girls.
society.context: It happened on a Sunday in September, at the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church. The outrage helped win support for the Civil Rights Act the next year.

society.text: A strong earthquake destroys much of the city of Skopje in Yugoslavia and kills more than a thousand people.
society.context: Skopje was later rebuilt with help from many countries, and the Japanese architect Kenzo Tange planned its new centre.

society.text: Martin Luther King Jr. tells a vast crowd at the Lincoln Memorial of his dream that his children will be judged by their character.
society.context: The speech closed the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, in August. About a quarter of a million people took part. It helped win support for the Civil Rights Act.

technology.text: The Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova becomes the first woman in space, orbiting the Earth in Vostok.
technology.context: She had worked in a textile factory and was a keen parachutist before she was chosen. She spent almost three days in orbit.

arts_culture.text: The Beatles release their first album, Please Please Me, in Britain, recorded in a single day.
arts_culture.context: Most of it was recorded in one long session in February at Abbey Road Studios in London. The album topped the British charts for many weeks.

arts_culture.text: BBC television broadcasts the first episode of Doctor Who, about a mysterious time traveller and his granddaughter.
arts_culture.context: It went out the day after the assassination of President Kennedy, and the BBC repeated it the next week because many people had missed it.

politics.text: Nelson Mandela is sentenced to life in prison at the end of the Rivonia Trial in South Africa.
politics.context: The sentence came in June. Mandela spent twenty-seven years in prison and became president of South Africa in 1994.

politics.text: President Lyndon Johnson signs the Civil Rights Act, outlawing segregation and discrimination in the United States.
politics.context: He signed it in July, after a long fight in the Senate. It ended legal segregation in public places and banned job discrimination.

politics.text: Labour narrowly wins the British general election, and Harold Wilson becomes prime minister after thirteen years of Conservative rule.
politics.context: Labour's majority was only four seats. Wilson promised to modernise Britain with the "white heat" of technology.

society.text: Tokyo hosts the Summer Olympic Games, the first held in Asia.
society.context: They opened in October. Japan used the Games to show how far it had recovered from the war.

technology.text: Japan opens the Tōkaidō Shinkansen, a high-speed railway running between Tokyo and Osaka at record speed.
technology.context: It opened in October, just before the Olympics. The bullet train ran at about two hundred kilometres an hour and became a model for fast trains around the world.

technology.text: BBC Two begins broadcasting in Britain, after a power cut forces the first night's launch to be put off.
technology.context: It was Britain's third television channel. It was the first to use the sharper line system that later became standard.

arts_culture.text: The British band the Beatles appear on The Ed Sullivan Show in New York and set off a wave of hysteria in America.
arts_culture.context: The appearance was in February. About seventy million Americans watched, a record for television at the time.

politics.text: Singapore leaves the Federation of Malaysia and becomes an independent republic under Lee Kuan Yew.
politics.context: It separated in August. Lee Kuan Yew wept on television, and Singapore grew into one of Asia's richest countries.

society.text: Civil rights marchers are beaten by state troopers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, on Bloody Sunday.
society.context: It happened in March. Television pictures of the attack shocked America and helped pass the Voting Rights Act.

technology.text: The Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov makes the first spacewalk, floating outside his spacecraft for about twelve minutes.
technology.context: He did it in March, tied to his spacecraft by a cable. He nearly could not get back in, because his suit had swollen in the vacuum.

arts_culture.text: Bob Dylan plugs in an electric guitar at the Newport Folk Festival, and is booed by part of the crowd.
arts_culture.context: It happened in July. Dylan's electric set marked the shift of folk music towards rock.

politics.text: Mao Zedong launches the Cultural Revolution in China, mobilising young Red Guards against his rivals.
politics.context: It began in May. The decade of upheaval led to millions of deaths and lasted until Mao's death in 1976.

society.text: England's footballers beat West Germany at Wembley Stadium to win the World Cup.
society.context: The final was in July and went to extra time. England won four goals to two, with a hat-trick from Geoff Hurst.

technology.text: A Soviet space probe makes the first soft landing on the Moon and sends back photographs from the surface.
technology.context: Luna 9 landed in the Ocean of Storms in February. Its pictures showed the ground was firm, which settled a fear that a lander would sink into deep dust.

arts_culture.text: The British band the Beatles release Revolver, an album that pushes pop music into studio experiments.
arts_culture.context: It came out in August. The album used tape loops and Indian instruments, and influenced rock music for years.

politics.text: Israel defeats Egypt, Jordan and Syria in the Six-Day War, capturing the Sinai, the West Bank and the Golan Heights.
politics.context: The war was fought in June and lasted six days. Israel roughly tripled the area it controlled.

society.text: Tens of thousands of young people gather in San Francisco for the "Summer of Love", centred on the Haight-Ashbury district.
society.context: It took place over the summer. The gathering made hippie culture a worldwide phenomenon.

society.text: Parliament partly decriminalises homosexuality between men in England and Wales, in the Sexual Offences Act.
society.context: The law applied only to adults, in private. It was one of several social reforms of the 1960s, along with the Abortion Act the same year.

society.text: Parliament passes the Abortion Act, allowing legal abortions in Britain under medical supervision.
society.context: The bill was put forward by the Liberal MP David Steel. It came into force the next year.

technology.text: The South African surgeon Christiaan Barnard performs the world's first human heart transplant in Cape Town.
technology.context: He operated in December. The patient lived for eighteen days.

arts_culture.text: The Beatles release Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, which many critics call one of the greatest albums ever.
arts_culture.context: It was released in June. Its cover and its sound influenced a generation of musicians.

politics.text: North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces launch the Tet Offensive across South Vietnam, shocking American public opinion.
politics.context: It began in late January, during the Tet holiday. The attack failed militarily, but it turned many Americans against the war.

politics.text: Soviet-led Warsaw Pact troops invade Czechoslovakia to crush the reforms of the Prague Spring.
politics.context: The invasion was in August. Soviet leaders ended the reforms, and Czechoslovakia stayed under hardline communist rule until 1989.

politics.text: The Conservative politician Enoch Powell gives his "Rivers of Blood" speech, attacking immigration to Britain.
politics.context: Edward Heath sacked him from the shadow cabinet the next day. The speech divided opinion across the country.

society.text: Student protests and a general strike shake France, almost bringing down President Charles de Gaulle's government.
society.context: The unrest peaked in May. Students occupied universities and about ten million workers went on strike.

society.text: The civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. is assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee.
society.context: He was shot in April while standing on a motel balcony. His death set off riots in many American cities.

technology.text: The American astronauts on the first crewed mission to orbit the Moon read from the Book of Genesis on Christmas Eve.
technology.context: The mission was Apollo 8, in December. The astronauts took the famous "Earthrise" photograph of the Earth over the Moon.

arts_culture.text: Stanley Kubrick's science-fiction film about a black monolith and the computer HAL premieres.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in April. The film's slow pace and visual effects were groundbreaking, and its meaning is still debated.

politics.text: Golda Meir becomes Prime Minister of Israel.
politics.context: She took office in March, after the death of Levi Eshkol. Meir was Israel's first female prime minister.

society.text: The Woodstock festival draws about four hundred thousand people to a farm in upstate New York.
society.context: It was held in August, in the rain and mud. Artists including Jimi Hendrix and Janis Joplin played.

society.text: The Open University is founded in Britain, to offer degrees by television, radio and post to adults.
society.context: It was a favourite project of Prime Minister Harold Wilson. It took no entry exams, and its first students began in 1971.

technology.text: The first message is sent over ARPANET, the computer network that grew into the internet.
technology.context: It was sent between computers at UCLA and Stanford in October. The system crashed after the first two letters of the word "LOGIN".

arts_culture.text: The Beatles release Abbey Road, whose cover shows them crossing a London street.
arts_culture.context: It was released in September. The cover photograph was taken in minutes, on a zebra crossing outside the Abbey Road studios.

politics.text: East Pakistan wins independence from Pakistan, with Indian help, after a bloody war, and becomes Bangladesh.
politics.context: The Liberation War ended in December. Bangladesh was recognised as a new country.

society.text: Swiss men vote in a national referendum to give women the right to vote in federal elections.
society.context: The referendum was held in February. Swiss women could now vote in federal elections, later than in almost every other European country.

society.text: President Richard Nixon takes the United States off the gold standard, ending the fixed exchange rates set up after the Second World War.
society.context: He announced it on television in August, along with a freeze on wages and prices. It became known as the Nixon shock, and the dollar has floated freely ever since.

technology.text: The American company Intel releases the first microprocessor, a fingernail-sized chip holding a whole computer processor.
technology.context: The chip was the 4004, designed for a Japanese calculator company, Busicom. It held about 2,300 transistors and came out in November.

technology.text: The American programmer Ray Tomlinson sends the first email between two computers on a network, in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
technology.context: He also chose the @ sign to separate the user's name from the computer's.

arts_culture.text: The former Beatle John Lennon releases Imagine, an album whose title song pictures a world without possessions or borders.
arts_culture.context: It came out in September. The song became Lennon's best-known solo work.

politics.text: American president Richard Nixon visits Beijing and meets Mao Zedong, opening relations with China.
politics.context: It happened in February. The visit ended more than two decades of hostility between the two countries.

politics.text: British paratroopers shoot dead thirteen civil rights marchers in Derry, in an event known as Bloody Sunday.
politics.context: The marchers were protesting against internment without trial. The killings pushed support towards the IRA and deepened the Troubles.

society.text: Palestinian gunmen take Israeli athletes hostage at the Munich Olympic Games, and eleven of them are killed.
society.context: The Munich massacre took place in September. It shocked the world and led to much tighter security at later Games.

technology.text: Atari releases Pong, one of the first successful video games, in an arcade in California.
technology.context: It was released in November. Pong helped start the video game industry.

arts_culture.text: Francis Ford Coppola's film The Godfather, based on Mario Puzo's novel about a Mafia family, is released.
arts_culture.context: It was released in March. It won the Oscar for Best Picture and is often listed among the greatest films.

politics.text: General Augusto Pinochet's army seizes power in Chile, and President Salvador Allende dies in the presidential palace.
politics.context: The coup took place in September. Pinochet ruled as a dictator for seventeen years.

politics.text: Egypt and Syria launch a surprise attack on Israel on the holy day of Yom Kippur.
politics.context: The war began in October. Israel recovered and won, but the surprise shocked the country.

politics.text: Britain, Ireland and Denmark join the European Economic Community, the forerunner of the European Union.
politics.context: Edward Heath had won Britain's entry after French vetoes in 1963 and 1967. Britain voted in a referendum to stay in two years later.

society.text: Arab oil producers cut supplies to countries that backed Israel in the Yom Kippur War, causing fuel queues and price shocks.
society.context: The oil embargo began in October. The price of oil roughly quadrupled and caused an economic crisis.

technology.text: The Motorola engineer Martin Cooper makes the first handheld mobile phone call, on a street in New York.
technology.context: It was in April. He rang a rival at Bell Labs.

arts_culture.text: Queen Elizabeth II opens the Sydney Opera House, with sail-like roofs designed by the Danish architect Jørn Utzon.
arts_culture.context: It opened in October. Utzon had left the project years earlier and did not attend.

politics.text: Army officers overthrow the dictatorship in Lisbon, and people put carnations in soldiers' rifles.
politics.context: The Carnation Revolution happened on the twenty-fifth of April. It was almost bloodless, and it ended nearly fifty years of dictatorship in Portugal.

politics.text: Greek officers stage a coup in Cyprus, and Turkey sends troops to invade the island days later, splitting it in two.
politics.context: The coup in July aimed to unite Cyprus with Greece. Turkish forces took the north, and the island has been divided ever since.

society.text: Muhammad Ali beats George Foreman in the "Rumble in the Jungle", in Kinshasa, in Zaire.
society.context: The fight was in October. Ali used his "rope-a-dope" tactic to win back the heavyweight title.

technology.text: American and French researchers find the skeleton of an early human relative, nicknamed Lucy, in Ethiopia.
technology.context: The find was in November. She was named after a Beatles song.

arts_culture.text: The Swedish pop group ABBA wins the Eurovision Song Contest with "Waterloo", in Brighton, England.
arts_culture.context: They won in April. The win launched ABBA to worldwide fame.

politics.text: North Vietnamese tanks enter Saigon, ending the Vietnam War, and South Vietnam's government surrenders.
politics.context: It happened on the last day of April. The fall of the city ended the Vietnam War, and the country was reunified under communist rule.

politics.text: The Khmer Rouge enter Phnom Penh, beginning Pol Pot's brutal rule over Cambodia.
politics.context: They entered the capital in April. Their rule killed about a quarter of Cambodia's people in the next four years.

politics.text: Margaret Thatcher beats Edward Heath to become leader of Britain's Conservative Party, the first woman to lead a major party.
politics.context: Heath had lost two elections in one year. She became prime minister four years later.

society.text: Muhammad Ali beats Joe Frazier in the "Thrilla in Manila", one of the greatest fights in boxing history.
society.context: It was held in October. Frazier's corner stopped the fight.

society.text: Sweden passes a law ending its state programme of eugenic sterilisation, which had sterilised thousands without free consent.
society.context: The new law took effect in 1976. About sixty-three thousand people were sterilised under the old laws, mostly women, many under pressure or by force. Sweden later paid compensation.

technology.text: Bill Gates and Paul Allen found Microsoft in Albuquerque, New Mexico, to write software for the Altair personal computer.
technology.context: They founded it in April. Microsoft grew into one of the world's most valuable companies.

arts_culture.text: Steven Spielberg's film Jaws, about a shark terrorising a New England beach town, opens and becomes the first summer blockbuster.
arts_culture.context: It opened in June. It was a huge success and created the summer blockbuster.

politics.text: Schoolchildren protest against Afrikaans-language teaching in Soweto, and police open fire, igniting a nationwide uprising.
politics.context: The Soweto uprising began on the sixteenth of June. Hundreds of people were killed, and the protests spread across South Africa.

society.text: The Romanian gymnast Nadia Comăneci scores the first perfect mark in Olympic gymnastics, at the Montreal Games.
society.context: The Games were in July. The scoreboard showed 1.00, as it could not display a ten.

technology.text: Britain and France begin the first supersonic passenger flights with Concorde.
technology.context: Services began in January. Concorde flew at about twice the speed of sound, and was retired in 2003.

technology.text: Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak found Apple Computer, in a garage in California.
technology.context: They founded it in April. Apple went on to launch the Apple II, one of the first mass-market home computers.

arts_culture.text: The British punk band the Sex Pistols swear on live television in London, causing a national scandal.
arts_culture.context: The interview was broadcast in December. The band was banned by many venues and record labels.

politics.text: Egyptian president Anwar Sadat visits Jerusalem, the first Arab leader to go to Israel.
politics.context: He went in November. His trip led to the Camp David Accords and a peace treaty between Egypt and Israel.

society.text: A huge power cut plunges New York City into darkness, followed by looting and fires.
society.context: The blackout was in July and lasted about a day. Looting and arson broke out in many neighbourhoods.

technology.text: NASA launches two Voyager probes on a grand tour of the outer planets.
technology.context: They were launched in August and September. Voyager 1 later became the first spacecraft to leave the solar system.

arts_culture.text: George Lucas's space adventure Star Wars opens in American cinemas.
arts_culture.context: It opened in May. It became one of the highest-earning films ever made and started a huge franchise.

politics.text: The Shah of Iran flees, and the Ayatollah Khomeini returns from exile in Paris to replace the monarchy with an Islamic republic.
politics.context: The revolution succeeded in February. It created a religious state and led to the American embassy hostage crisis.

politics.text: Soviet troops invade Afghanistan to prop up its communist government.
politics.context: The invasion began in late December. It led to a ten-year war, and Soviet forces left in 1989.

politics.text: Margaret Thatcher wins the British general election and becomes the first woman prime minister of the United Kingdom.
politics.context: The Conservatives won after the strikes of the Winter of Discontent. She stayed in office for eleven years.

society.text: A reactor at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania partly melts down, changing America's nuclear debate for good.
society.context: The accident happened in March. No one was killed, but it badly damaged public support for nuclear power in the United States.

technology.text: The Japanese company Sony launches the Walkman, a portable cassette player, in Tokyo.
technology.context: It went on sale in July. The Walkman made personal, portable music possible.

arts_culture.text: Francis Ford Coppola's Vietnam war film Apocalypse Now, based on a novella by Joseph Conrad, shares the top prize at Cannes.
arts_culture.context: It premiered in May. The film's troubled production later became the subject of a documentary.

politics.text: Iraq invades Iran, starting a war that lasts eight years.
politics.context: It began in September. The war lasted eight years and caused hundreds of thousands of deaths.

politics.text: Lech Wałęsa leads striking shipyard workers in Gdańsk to found Solidarity, the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc.
politics.context: It was founded in August after strikes at the Lenin Shipyard. Solidarity helped bring down communist rule in Poland nine years later.

society.text: A volcano erupts in the state of Washington, killing dozens and blasting the top off the mountain.
society.context: It erupted on 18 May. Fifty-seven people died, and the blast flattened forests across about six hundred square kilometres.

society.text: The former Beatle John Lennon is shot dead outside his home in New York City.
society.context: He was killed in December by a fan, Mark David Chapman. Lennon was forty.

technology.text: The World Health Organization declares that smallpox has been wiped out from the world.
technology.context: The declaration was made in May. Smallpox was the first human disease to be eradicated.

arts_culture.text: The Italian writer Umberto Eco publishes his medieval murder mystery The Name of the Rose.
arts_culture.context: It became an international bestseller.

politics.text: Egyptian president Anwar Sadat is assassinated by soldiers during a military parade in Cairo.
politics.context: He was killed in October by soldiers who opposed his peace with Israel. Hosni Mubarak became president.

society.text: Prince Charles marries Lady Diana Spencer at Saint Paul's Cathedral, in front of a worldwide television audience.
society.context: The wedding was in July. About seven hundred and fifty million people are thought to have watched on television.

technology.text: IBM launches its Personal Computer, setting the standard for desktop computers.
technology.context: It was launched in August. The IBM PC's design shaped most later personal computers.

arts_culture.text: The music channel MTV launches in the United States, opening with the video for Video Killed the Radio Star.
arts_culture.context: It launched in August. MTV changed the music business by making videos as important as songs.

politics.text: Israel invades Lebanon, aiming to destroy Palestinian forces, and reaches the outskirts of Beirut.
politics.context: It began in June. Israeli forces besieged Beirut and drove out the Palestine Liberation Organization.
